item.title: Lady Bears Sweep Capitan as Otero County Volleyball Teams Struggle
item.description:
Otero County- Cloudcroft provided the lone bright spot for area volleyball this week, sweeping Capitan Thursday night while Alamogordo, Tularosa and Mescalero Apache all came up short.

The Lady Bears survived a marathon opening set, edging Capitan 30-28, then pulled away in the next two for a 25-22, 25-18 straight-set win. The victory lifts Cloudcroft to 11-8 overall and 3-2 in district play.

Cloudcroft returns home Saturday to host Lordsburg, then welcomes Mescalero Apache on Tuesday.

The Lady Tigers were swept by Organ Mountain earlier this week, 25-16, 25-13, 25-20. Alamogordo kept the third set close but couldn't force a fourth.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 6-14 overall and 0-6 in district. The Lady Tigers host Mayfield on Saturday.

Tularosa had a tough week, losing twice in two days.

In the first, Ruidoso beat the Lady Cats in four sets, 25-15, 18-25, 25-9, 25-14. Tularosa answered a lopsided first set by taking the second, but Ruidoso controlled the rest of the match.

Thursday at Dexter, the Lady Cats pushed every set but lost in three, 25-23, 25-20, 26-24. The third set went to extra points before Dexter closed it out.

Tularosa falls to 5-16 overall and 0-4 in district. The Lady Cats host NMMI on Tuesday.

Lordsburg rolled past the Lady Chiefs Thursday, 25-2, 25-6, 25-10. Mescalero Apache scored more in each successive set but couldn't slow Lordsburg.

The Lady Chiefs fall to 3-17 overall and 0-6 in district. They play at Cloudcroft on Tuesday.

Saturday, Oct. 31

Tuesday, Nov. 3

item.title: Endorsement: Alamogordo Needs a Leader Again at the Roundhouse, Grace Nagamine Is That Leader
item.description:
True Conservatives believe in results over rhetoric, accountability for public money, and leaders who answer to their neighbors rather than to political machines.

By those standards, the best choice in House District 51 this year is not the Republican on the ballot. It is independent, Grace Nagamine.

What real leadership looked like

Alamogordo doesn’t have to imagine what effective representation looks like. We once had it.

Ron Griggs served as our mayor, ran a local business, and then represented Otero County in the state Senate for more than a decade.

He was a Republican in a Democratic Legislature, and he still delivered:

• Wildfire prevention: In 2023, his bill banning prescribed burns on Red Flag warning days became law. Griggs credited the Legislature with passing it by unanimous, bipartisan vote.

• Economic development: He sponsored legislation lowering taxes on construction costs for large economic development projects, and legislation letting more small restaurants sell spirits.• Infrastructure: Local coverage noted his focus on job creation and his success securing capital funding for roads, public infrastructure, and other district projects.

Griggs never stopped being a conservative. He also never confused being loud with being effective. He built relationships across the aisle because that is how real dollars beyond standard outlays, and laws reach rural New Mexico.

Since his departure, that kind of true collaborative leadership has been missing from Alamogordo’s delegation.

Four years of a different approach

Rep. John Block has held the House District 51 seat since 2023. He moved here and flipped his alliances and recreated an identity taking advantage of local ideologies, (he interned for Martin Heinrich Democrat and worked for the Liberal Mayor Keller Campaign in Albuquerque while younger.) He has since whitewashed those facts and removed them from his public profiles. 

His defenders say a Republican can’t get anything done in a Democratic Legislature. Senator Griggs proved otherwise for years, and Block’s own colleagues prove it today:

• Other Republicans passed bills. In 2026, 25 of 26 House Republicans had a bill signed into law.

• He ranked near the bottom. Block ranked 19th of 26 by the share of his measures that passed.

• He led none of his signed bills. Three signed bills carry his name, and other legislators led all three.

• His own bills died early. All 33 measures he brought himself failed, most in their first committee.

His mailer claims more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County. That is the standard share of capital outlay every House member receives, added up over four years. Block chose his projects, then voted against the bills that funded them in 2023, 2025, and 2026.

In 2025 he also introduced a new 3.75% tax on renewable energy production. The free-market Southwest Public Policy Institute opposed it as harmful to consumers. That cost would have landed on PNM ratepayers, the same families who opened doubled and tripled PNM bills this year.

The difference is not ideology. Griggs and Block are both Republicans.

The difference is that one treated the Legislature as a place to build results for Alamogordo, and the other treats it as a stage for partisan fights.

Otero County has paid for that in lost opportunities.

Grace Nagamine: back to results

Grace Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident and a member of Mountain View Church for more than a decade. She survived homelessness and domestic violence, worked as a certified nursing assistant, cared for family, and founded Royal Angels to serve children with special needs.

Her platform is specific and in writing:

• Energy: She released a policy brief backing responsible oil and gas production and defending the permanent fund savings law.

• Holloman and veterans: She comes from an Air Force family and has made housing for military families a priority.

• Infrastructure: She has pledged to work with city leadership to bring state dollars to the roads, water lines, and sewer lines neglected for two decades.

• Transparency: She will publish every capital outlay request she makes.

• Partnership: She has committed to working with any legislator, Republican or Democrat, who will help Otero County, including regional partnership with District 33 state leadership and other leaders within the state

Grace Policy Statements:
https://graceforhd51.org/policy-statements/

Grace Platform and Policy Pillars:
https://graceforhd51.org/issues

That is the Griggs model: local roots, a plan, and the willingness to work with anyone to get it done.

Republicans, Democrats, and independents together

Nagamine’s support crosses party lines, the way a district representative’s should.

For those in the conservative community that are not convinced two Republicans who led Alamogordo City Hall are among those backing her.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, a Republican and former Alamogordo City Manager:

“I’m tired of divisive politics. New Mexico has fallen behind in too many areas, and I believe much of that comes from our inability to work together. Some of the deepest divisions aren’t even between political parties anymore. They’re within our own parties. We’ve become so focused on our differences that we’ve lost sight of the goals we share.

Somewhere along the way, we’ve confused fighting with leadership. Having served in local government, I know firsthand that progress requires relationships, cooperation, and the willingness to work with people who don’t always share your views. You can stand firm in your convictions without standing in the way of progress.

I know Grace Nagamine. She’s a fighter, but she also understands the value of teamwork. She knows the difference between fighting for people and simply fighting with people. Grace is willing to put differences aside, find common ground, and work toward what matters most: improving the lives of the people she represents. That’s why I’m supporting her.”

— Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, Republican, former Alamogordo City Manager

Susan Payne, a Republican and former Mayor of Alamogordo:

“For years, I’ve watched Santa Fe fail to address the issues that matter most to New Mexico families: our children’s education, their safety, and the growing concerns about crime in our communities.

As a former mayor, I know firsthand the consequences of failed policies. I had to lead our community through one of its darkest moments, the death of a police officer in the line of duty. It’s a tragedy that stays with you and one that strengthened my belief that our state must do better. Yet we continue to operate under a constitutional amendment that I believe has made it harder to hold dangerous criminals accountable and keep them off our streets.

Year after year, we hear the same promises, witness the same political division, and hope that something will finally change. But the issues remain, and our communities continue to pay the price.

That’s why I believe it’s time for a different approach. I believe Grace has what it takes to be a truly independent voice in Santa Fe. Someone who can work across party lines, find common ground, and put the needs of New Mexicans ahead of political agendas.

We cannot afford another year of the same excuses and the same results. Our state deserves leaders who recognize where we’ve fallen short and, more importantly, are willing to do something about it.

I’m supporting Grace because I believe it’s time to stop talking about change and start making it happen.”

— Susan Payne, Republican, former Mayor of Alamogordo

Republicans have joined Democrats and independents knocking on doors for her across the district.

They don’t agree on everything. But they agree Alamogordo deserves a representative who delivers - and are supportive of Grace Nagamine. With an army of over 100 individuals knocking on doors, dropping flyers and making phone calls she has support from grass roots neighbors not big corporations nor multiple major PACs. 

The fair objection

Some conservatives will say a vote for an independent weakens the Republican caucus, and that Block reliably votes the conservative line. 

But a reliable no vote is not the same as getting results for the local Alamogordo community. One House seat will not change which party controls the chamber

It will decide whether Alamogordo has an effective voice inside it.

Our endorsement

Alamogordo once had leaders who put this community ahead of party fights. It’s time to have one once again

Grace Nagamine is the voice Alamogordo needs now.

Early voting is underway, and Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Vote today.

This editorial was approved unanimously by the New Mexico Conservative News editorial advisory board, whose members include two Republicans, two Democrats, one Libertarian, and one member who declined to state a party.

item.title: Tigers Roll Into Playoffs After Friday Win on Four-Game Win Streak
item.description:
CHAPARRAL, N.M. — Alamogordo ran for eight touchdowns and routed Chaparral 56-7 on Friday night. The win closed the regular season with a fourth straight victory and a 6-4 record, 5-2 in District 2-5A. Seven different Tigers reached the end zone, and Alamogordo led 35-7 at halftime.

The win caps one of the sharpest in-season turnarounds in recent program history. Alamogordo was 2-4 after a 54-19 home loss to Artesia on Sept. 25 and has not lost since.

Tigers run wild at Chaparral

Senior Nathaniel Cereceres opened the scoring on a 1-yard run with 9:08 left in the first quarter. With 2:36 left in the quarter, Qymani Patterson broke a 93-yard touchdown run for a 14-0 lead.

Leyton Niland scored from 23 yards out early in the second quarter to make it 21-0. Cereceres followed with an 80-yard run at the 4:38 mark for a 28-0 lead. Chaparral's only score came 56 seconds later, when Isaiah Torres hit Zahid Chavez on a 72-yard pass. Tristan Bowman answered with a 20-yard run with 33 seconds left in the half.

Samuel Strong opened the second half scoring with a 67-yard run at 7:23 of the third quarter. Ryan Sebring added a 2-yard score with 17 seconds left in the quarter and a 41-yard run midway through the fourth. Kicker Russell made all eight extra points.

Where the Tigers stand

Alamogordo finishes third in District 2-5A, behind champion Roswell and Artesia. The Tigers' only district losses came to those two teams. Artesia holds the head-to-head tiebreaker from its Sept. 25 win.

• Roswell clinched the district title and finished 9-1 overall and 7-0 in district play after beating Goddard 42-35 on Friday.• Artesia is 5-4 and 5-1 in district play, with its finale at Mayfield on Saturday.• Gadsden was 6-3 and 3-3 in district play before Friday's game at Deming.• Goddard finished 4-6 and 3-4.

Statewide, NMPreps' Week 11 rankings put Alamogordo No. 20 among all 88 teams and No. 4 in Class 5A. The Albuquerque Journal's Oct. 26 coaches poll had the Tigers seventh in 5A.

Playoff picture

The NMAA releases the Class 5A bracket this weekend, which will set the Tigers' first-round opponent. New Mexico has no separate district playoff. District finishes and statewide rankings feed a single state bracket. The first round is Nov. 6-7, quarterfinals Nov. 13-14 and semifinals Nov. 20-21. The state championship is Nov. 28.

In recent seasons the 11-man brackets have held 12 teams. The top four seeds get first-round byes, and seeds 5 through 12 play the opening weekend. Roswell, Piedra Vista and Artesia sit firmly ahead of the Tigers in both polls, so Alamogordo projects to play next weekend rather than rest.

This is Alamogordo's first season in Class 5A. The NMAA's 2026-27 realignment moved the Tigers and Chaparral down from 6A into District 2-5A.

The turnaround

Head coach AJ Cisco's team opened the season with a 41-33 win over Santa Fe. A 28-20 loss at Clovis and a loss at Organ Mountain followed. In district play, the Tigers lost to Roswell, won 28-27 in overtime at Goddard, then fell 54-19 to Artesia.

The swing began on homecoming night, Oct. 2, with a 24-19 win over Mayfield. On Oct. 16 the Tigers handed Gadsden its first home loss, 23-14, rushing for a then season-high 372 yards. They routed Deming 49-7 on Oct. 22, then put up their highest point total of the year at Chaparral. Over the final four games, Alamogordo outscored opponents 152-47.

Against the last three years

Six wins is the most for an Alamogordo regular season in more than a decade. Our local preview last fall noted that a 6-4 finish would be the program's best since 2011. The Tigers went 11-19 combined from 2023 to 2025:

• 2023: 5-5 in District 4-6A, reaching .500 with a season-ending win over Organ Mountain.• 2024: 2-8, ending a five-game skid with a 62-22 win over Clovis in the finale.• 2025: 4-6 overall and 1-5 in District 3-6A, closing with a 48-43 loss at Clovis.

This season ran in the opposite direction from 2025. Last year's Tigers started 4-1 and dropped their last five. This group stumbled early and enters November on a four-game winning streak.

Player spotlights

Nathaniel Cereceres, Sr., RB/LB (5-11, 195): scored twice at Chaparral, including the 80-yarder, and also scored in the Gadsden win.

Leyton Niland, Sr., RB/OLB (5-8, 160): added a 23-yard touchdown Friday after scoring at Gadsden.

 Qymani Patterson: delivered the longest play of the night, the 93-yard run.

 Samuel Strong and Tristan Bowman, Srs., WR/FS: each scored on the ground.

Ryan Sebring: scored twice in the second half.• Russell, K: went 8-for-8 on extra points.

 Tanner Nowaczck, Sr., TE/DE (6-2, 185): scored in the Gadsden win.

 Bryson Bloom, Sr., RB/LB: ran for 205 yards in last year's finale at Clovis.

Around Otero County

Tularosa shut out Cobre 12-0 on Friday. The Wildcats finish the regular season 6-4 overall and 2-2 in district play.

Stay tuned to Alamogordo Town

item.title: Endorsement: For Senate District 33, Liam Griffin Has Already Shown Up
item.description:
Senate District 33 stretches across parts of Otero, Lincoln and Chaves counties, including parts of Alamogordo, Ruidoso and the ranch country of Lincoln County. On Nov. 3, voters there will elect a state senator for the first time since Sen. Nicholas Paul resigned for health reasons in October 2025. Not every Alamogordo address falls in this district, so check your sample ballot.

Both candidates are serious, decent people with strong ties to this region. That makes this a harder call than most. 

After weighing their records and their reasons for running, we endorse Liam Griffin.

The incumbent

Sen. Rex Wilson, a Republican rancher from Ancho, was not elected to this seat. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham appointed him in January 2026 from a list of nominees submitted by county commissions. Chaves County nominated him unanimously. He took office days before the session began.

His background is substantial:

Local government: He served as a Lincoln County commissioner from 1997 to 2003.

Health care: He spent 18 years as a health care administrator, including as southern region director for Presbyterian Medical Services, overseeing programs across Chaves, Lincoln and Otero counties.

Ranching: The New Mexico Cattle Growers Association named him 2017 Cattleman of the Year.

 Youth: He founded Camp Sierra Blanca at Fort Stanton, an alternative education program for at-risk young people.

Fairness requires saying plainly that his short time in Santa Fe has been productive. His Medicare supplement open enrollment bill, Senate Bill 21, passed the Senate 36-0 and was signed into law in March. That is more than some legislators manage in a full term and as a novice legislator out performs state Rep John Block in effectiveness as a Republican.

Before his appointment, he described the seat as one meant “to support local government, not the other way around.”

We have no quarrel with Rex Wilson’s character or his competence.

Our endorsement rests on something else: what this district needs most right now, and who has proven he will deliver it.

The challenger

Liam Griffin, listed in state election records as William Griffin, was born in Albuquerque and raised in a modest family with four siblings. He built a career in telecommunications in the United States and Europe, then went to law school after watching the legal system used against a member of his own family. He came home to New Mexico in 2010 and has practiced law since. Today he practices in Ruidoso, often for clients who cannot afford a lawyer at market rates.

When the floods hit Ruidoso, Griffin did not wait for an office to act. He took on legal work for people affected by the floods, much of it without pay. In 2024 the 12th Judicial District Pro Bono Committee named him Pro Bono Attorney of the Year for that work.

That is the heart of our endorsement. Long before he asked for a single vote, Griffin spent his own time helping his neighbors through one of the worst disasters this region has faced in years. The burn scar and flood recovery in Lincoln County will be a central job for whoever holds this seat. Griffin knows it from the inside, one case at a time.

What he is running on

Griffin calls himself “a pragmatist, not a partisan,” and his campaign centers on the kitchen-table problems voters across this district raise:

Affordability: Working families struggling to cover food, housing and health care.

Health care access: Parents who should not have to choose between a doctor’s visit and groceries, in a region short on providers.

Jobs and education: Opportunity close to home, so young people who grow up here can build a life here.

Government that listens: Representation for voters who feel unheard by Santa Fe.

Griffin is a Democrat, and many of our readers will pause at that. We understand. But this seat should belong to someone who answers to Alamogordo, Ruidoso and the ranch communities of this district, not to a caucus

Griffin’s pro bono work did not ask about anyone’s party. He has spent years helping whoever walked through his office door in trouble.

A lawyer who holds government accountable

A senator’s job is to write laws and to hold state government to them. Griffin brings training for both. He holds a law degree and has practiced law in New Mexico for 16 years, reading statutes, arguing them in court and seeing where they fail ordinary people. That is direct preparation for drafting legislation that works the first time.

He has also been willing to take on government itself when it fell short of the openness the law requires as he did in Ruidoso previously in a first amendment case.

A senator who has gone to court for public transparency will not need to be persuaded that voters deserve to see how decisions are made in Santa Fe.

In our board’s experience, he is personable and approachable, he listens before he argues, and he looks for the deal that solves the problem rather than the fight that makes the headline. In a Legislature where results depend on relationships across the aisle, that temperament is an asset to the whole district.

The fair objection

Wilson’s supporters will say he has already passed a law, brings decades of public and health care leadership, and fits a district that has elected Republicans. All true. They will add that Griffin’s campaign website lays out priorities rather than detailed bills. That is a fair criticism, and we urge him to fix it if elected by putting his plans in writing early and often.

But Wilson holds this seat by appointment, not by election. On Nov. 3, voters decide for themselves who represents them for the first time since the seat came open. We believe the candidate who has already done the hard, unpaid work of rebuilding lives in this district has earned the chance to do it in the Senate.

Our endorsement

Senate District 33 needs a senator who knows what recovery looks like on the ground and who will fight for affordable health care and opportunity at home

Liam Griffin has shown us who he is when no one was watching. That is the kind of leader we want in Santa Fe.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Make a plan and vote.

item.title: In Memory of Helen Elaine Van Tassel
item.description:
Helen Elaine Van Tassel, 97, passed away peacefully on October 17, 2026, leaving behind a lifetime of memories, love, and a family who will forever cherish her.

Elaine lived a long and meaningful life, devoted to her family and the people around her. She was a loving wife, mother, grandmother, great grandmother, and great-great grandmother whose legacy will continue through the many generations she leaves behind.

Elaine was a crafty and creative woman who enjoyed keeping busy and sharing her talents with others. She also enjoyed volunteering at Animal Rescue Thrift Store with her friend of 20 years, Dottie Eisler, and spending time at the senior center where she could visit with others, stay active, and enjoy the friendships she made. Elaine was a lifetime member of the Moose Lodge and Fraternal order of Eagles. Her willingness to give her time and her love for staying connected with her community were special parts of who she was.

Above all, family was an important part of Elaine's life. She leaves behind her beloved husband of 76 years, Johnny Van Tassel; her brother, Wilbur Adams; her children, Terry Van Tassel, Doris Foster and her husband Mike, and Alan Van Tassel and his wife Rafaela; her grandchildren, Joe Webb, Jennifer Vickrey, June Harris and her spouse Lloyd Vega, Rebecca Earley, Matthew Foster and his wife Rose; honorary granddaughter, Rachel Black; 14 great grandchildren; 10 great-great grandchildren; 2 nieces.

She was preceded in death by her twin sister, Ellen Lorraine Meno; her daughter, Johnine Harris; daughter-in-law, Elosie Van Tassel; great grandson Jesse Webb.

At 97 years old, Elaine leaves behind a remarkable family legacy spanning five generations. Her life was a testament to the enduring bonds of family, the value of friendship, and the importance of finding joy in everyday moments.

Though she will be deeply missed, the love Elaine gave, the memories she created, and the generations she helped shape will live on in the hearts of those who knew and loved her.

Her family will forever hold her close in their hearts, grateful for the years they shared and the love that will never fade.

Elaine’s life was long, her family was her legacy, and her love will live on for generations to come.

item.title: In Memory of Teresita Baldonado Hutchings
item.description:
Teresita Baldonado Hutchings passed away peacefully in her home on October 21, 2026 at the age of 98. Life-Long resident of Tularosa, she was born Teresita Lucila Baldonado on August 19, 1928, the youngest of eleven children to Juan and Virginia Baldonado. Teresita’s Great Grandmother, Antonia Baca was one of the founders of Tularosa in 1862.

Teresita was the last surviving member of the Tularosa High School class of 1946.

Well known for her strong singing voice and a member of many choirs over decades at St. Francis de Paula Church in Tularosa. Teresita and her three older sisters were recruited by Father Albert Braun to sing at his masses he held in Mescalero at the many cow camps of the Mescalero’s.

Teresita is preceded in death by her parents, Juan and Virginia, her brothers Luis (Clara), Arturo (Father Felipe), Juan (Francis), Jose (Betty), Ramon (Viola); sisters, Anita (Homer), Virginia (Ross), Mary (Henry), Elisa (Raymond); her husbands, Lyle Danke, Samuel Torres, and Harvey Hutchings; her daughter Christina, and granddaughter Karen.

She is survived by her sister Elena, son Robert (Diana), and many nieces and nephews.

Services will be on November 4, 2026 at St. Francis de Paula church, Rosary and viewing at 10:00 am, mass at 10:30 am with internment at Sacred Heart Cemetery following the mass.

In lieu of sending flowers or cards, please donate to Jornada Research Institute in Teresita’s name.

item.title: Keep Our Schools Off the Partisan Ballot: Why We Recommend No on Amendment 2
item.description:
Constitutional Amendment 2 is the quietest question on Tuesday’s ballot. It deletes a single sentence from the New Mexico Constitution: “All school elections shall be held at different times from partisan elections.”

Supporters call that sentence a relic.

We see it as one of the last walls between our children’s schools and the party politics that have divided this state and this country.

At a time when partisan divides keep growing, this is the wrong moment to tear it down. We recommend a NO vote.

What the amendment actually does

Since statehood, the constitution has required school elections to be held separately from partisan elections. Today, under the 2018 Local Election Act, school board races are held alongside other nonpartisan local elections, apart from the races for governor, Congress and the Legislature.

Amendment 2, passed by the Legislature as Senate Joint Resolution 1, strikes that requirement entirely. It adds no new language and no limits. That would allow two things:

Bond and mill-levy questions: School districts could place them on the November general-election ballot in even years.

School board races: The Legislature could, by ordinary statute, move school board elections onto the same ballot as partisan races.

The amendment does not itself make school board races partisan. But it removes the constitutional barrier that keeps them separate, and leaves the rest to whatever a future Legislature decides.

Why separation matters

The framers of New Mexico’s 1910 constitution set school elections apart for their own reasons. Their decision has served the state well for a different one: it keeps school board races about schools.

When a school board candidate shares a ballot with candidates for governor and Congress, several things tend to follow:

Party labels fill the information gap. Voters who know little about a school board race tend to rely on whatever cues are around them. On a ballot full of Ds and Rs, that cue is party, even if the board race itself carries no label.

Party machinery moves in. Campaigns organized for top-of-ticket races recruit, slate and promote down-ballot candidates who fit their side. School boards become one more front in the same fight.

National issues crowd out local ones. Even-year campaigns are dominated by national arguments and national money. Questions about reading scores, bus routes and building repairs get buried under them.

School races fall to the bottom of a long ballot. Otero County voters already face two full pages of contests in some years. Voters who are tired or rushed skip races at the bottom, and school questions would sit there.

We have spent this election season arguing that the most effective public servants are the ones who put community ahead of party

Grace Nagamine is running as an independent precisely because, as she says, a broken water system and an overwhelmed child-welfare system “don’t belong to one party.

Neither do our schools. School boards are among the few places left where neighbors with different politics still sit at the same table to solve a shared problem.

We should protect that, not merge it into the partisan ballot.

The case for yes, fairly stated

Supporters make real arguments, and voters deserve to hear them:

Cost: Stand-alone school elections cost districts $125,000 to $250,000 each. Alamogordo Public Schools held its last bond and mill-levy election as a stand-alone all-mail special election in May 2023. Statewide, districts held 12 such elections in 2024 and 2025, according to the Legislature’s fiscal analysis.

Turnout: The same analysis says studies show turnout in off-cycle school board elections can be less than half that of on-cycle elections. Low turnout can give small organized groups outsized influence.

Bipartisan support: The resolution passed the Senate 38–0 and the House 50–9. Voters approved related changes in 2008, 2010 and 2014, though compilation errors kept them from taking full effect.

Flexibility: Districts would keep the option of calling a special election when they need one.

These are legitimate points, especially on cost. If this amendment were limited to letting school bond and mill-levy questions appear on the November ballot, we would likely support it. Even the voter guide notes that a narrower alternative, allowing only bond questions on general ballots, was available.

Why the cost argument does not settle it

Saving a district up to $250,000 every few years is worth something.

But the price of this amendment is not measured only in dollars.

It is a permanent change to the constitution, made in the broadest possible way, to solve a problem that a narrower fix could have solved.

Higher turnout is a good thing. But turnout driven by a governor’s race is not the same as turnout from voters who came to decide who runs their schools. Many of those voters will reach the school questions knowing little about them, and the cues they fall back on will be partisan.

And while the Legislature that passed this amendment may have no plans to make school boards partisan, the amendment does not bind future Legislatures.

Once the constitutional wall is gone, keeping school races separate depends entirely on whichever majority holds power in Santa Fe.

A protection that can be removed by ordinary statute is not much of a protection.

A better path

Voting no does not lock New Mexico into expensive special elections forever. The Legislature can return with a narrower amendment that lets school bond and mill-levy questions ride the November ballot while keeping school board elections separate from partisan races. That would capture most of the savings and most of the turnout benefit without pulling school board races into the partisan cycle.

We would support that amendment. We encourage our legislators, including whoever wins in House District 51 and Senate District 33, to bring it forward in 2027.

Our recommendation

Our schools are not supposed to be red or blue. The people who run them should not be chosen on a ballot built around red and blue. Until the Legislature offers a narrower fix, the safer course is to keep the constitution’s wall in place.

Vote NO on Constitutional Amendment 2.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Amendment 2 appears on every Otero County ballot and passes with a simple majority of votes cast on the question. Questions on voting Tuesday visit NMVote.org or with the County Clerk at (575) 437-4942.

item.title: Our Ballot Question Recommendations: Yes to Transparency, No to a Paycheck Without Accountability
item.description:
Our endorsements this year have rested on a few plain principles. Government should be open about how it makes decisions. Public officials should be judged by results, not by party labels or noise. Taxpayer money deserves careful stewardship. And Alamogordo and Otero County deserve their fair share from Santa Fe.

Every Otero County ballot also carries four constitutional amendments, three statewide bond questions and, as the last item, a county economic development tax. They get less attention than the candidates, but they will shape state and county government for years. Here is how we recommend voting, and why each choice follows from the same principles behind our endorsements of Grace Nagamine in House District 51 and Liam Griffin in Senate District 33

Amendment 1: Governor’s vetoes — YES

Today, a bill sent to the governor in the last three days of a session dies if the governor simply does nothing. No explanation, no record, no chance for lawmakers to fix it. One estimate counts about 143 bills killed this way from 2014 to 2024, under governors of both parties.

Amendment 1 ends that. A bill would become law unless the governor vetoes it with a substantive written explanation within 20 days after the session ends, and every veto would require an explanation.

This is the transparency we have asked of every candidate. It was sponsored by Republicans and Democrats together and passed the House 66–0 and the Senate 38–0. Critics warn that “substantive explanation” is undefined and could invite lawsuits, and that a rush of last-minute bills could become law by default. Those are fair concerns, but the Legislature can define the standard by statute. A governor who kills a bill should have to tell the public why.

Amendment 2: School election timing — NO

This amendment deletes the constitutional requirement that school elections be held separately from partisan elections. It would let school districts put bond and mill-levy questions on the November ballot, and would let a future Legislature move school board races onto the same ballot as races for governor and Congress.

Supporters make a real case. Stand-alone school elections cost districts $125,000 to $250,000 each, and turnout in off-cycle school races can be less than half of on-cycle turnout. If the amendment were limited to bond and mill-levy questions, we would likely support it.

But it is not limited. It removes the wall between school boards and the partisan ballot entirely, leaving the rest to whichever majority holds power in Santa Fe. With partisan divides growing, our schools should be the last place we invite them. We explain our reasoning in full in a separate editorial. Vote no, and let the Legislature return with a narrower fix.

Amendment 3: University regents — YES

Today, governors appoint university regents with no required qualifications, and governors of both parties have filled those seats with friends and donors. Amendment 3 would create a nominating committee for each of the state’s ten universities, including NMSU, which governs NMSU-Alamogordo. Governors could appoint only from the committee’s list, the Senate would still confirm, and appointees could not have switched parties in the prior year to game the process.

Opponents argue that an unelected committee blurs accountability. We take that seriously, but the governor still appoints and the Senate still confirms. What changes is that the people running our universities would have to be qualified to do it. That is the same standard of competence over connections we have applied to the Legislature itself. It passed the House 67–0 and the Senate 34–7.

Amendment 4: Legislator pay — NO

New Mexico is the only state that pays its legislators no salary. Amendment 4 would pay each of them the state median household income, about $68,000 today, adjusted annually and beginning in 2029. The estimated cost is about $7.6 million a year.

We understand the appeal. Supporters say a salary would open the Legislature to working people who cannot afford to serve for free, and that is a real problem. Many of the candidates we admire most come from exactly that background.

But this amendment writes a paycheck without a job description. It sets pay above the national average for legislators, about $44,000, with no limit on outside income and no added service required beyond the existing 30- and 60-day sessions. It leaves open how benefits, pensions and per diem would be treated.

It also tilts the field toward incumbents. Sitting legislators would draw a salary while challengers give up income to run against them. This year we have endorsed two challengers who are running on their records of service, not their titles. A salary for incumbents would make races like theirs harder.

The amendment passed largely along party lines, 41–26 in the House and 23–19 in the Senate, and several Democrats voted no. A legislator salary may deserve a place in New Mexico’s future, but it should come with clear duties, real accountability and a fair field for challengers. This one does not.

Bond Questions 1, 2 and 3 — YES

All three bond questions were authorized by House Bill 248, which passed the House 65–0 and the Senate 38–0. The Legislative Finance Committee reports the package was sized to replace bonds being paid off, keeping the state’s bond tax rate flat rather than raising it.

Bond 1, senior facilities ($21.6 million): Includes $260,000 for vehicles for Otero County senior centers. Helping seniors stay connected and age at home is a priority we have backed throughout this campaign season.

Bond 2, libraries ($19.3 million): Funds materials for public, school, academic and tribal libraries. The Alamogordo Public Library, local school libraries and NMSU-Alamogordo are eligible to apply.

Bond 3, higher education ($352.2 million): Includes $1 million for NMSU-Alamogordo to replace keyed locks with electronic access control on every building, a direct investment in campus safety.

The New Mexico Business Coalition opposes all three. It estimates they cost about $46 a year per $100,000 of taxable value, and argues that rejecting them could lower property taxes. It also points out that Bonds 1 and 2 pay for vehicles, equipment and materials that may wear out before the 10-year debt is repaid. That is the strongest argument on the other side, and Bond 2 is the weakest of the three on those grounds.

Otero County receives only about $1.26 million of the $393 million package, and the New Mexico School for the Blind and Visually Impaired in Alamogordo receives nothing. That is a fair grievance, and it is exactly the kind of fight we expect our legislators to win next session. But voting these bonds down would not send one more dollar to Otero County. On balance, a tax-neutral package that funds senior transportation, campus security and local libraries deserves a yes.

County LEDA gross receipts tax — NO

The last question on the Otero County ballot asks voters to approve a new countywide gross receipts tax of one-eighth of one percent (0.125%) under the Local Economic Development Act. The money would fund economic development projects, and the county is using the state’s model ballot question, which also makes retail businesses, cultural facilities and arts and cultural districts eligible.

Supporters, including the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce, describe it as about a penny on an $8 purchase. They note that 83 New Mexico communities have LEDA ordinances, that awards must be approved by county ordinance in a public process, and that projects carry clawback provisions if promised jobs never come.

Economic development is a worthy goal. But voters are being asked to approve the money before anyone has shown them the plan. Two of the Republican leaders who endorsed Grace Nagamine put it best. Former City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez asked, “If this tax passes, what’s the plan?” Former Mayor Susan Payne said, “We need a strategy first, then determine how to fund it.” Neither objects to LEDA itself. Both object to taxing first and planning later.

The county’s books give voters more reason for caution:

Audit findings: The county’s fiscal 2025 audit reported six findings, three of them repeats, including material weaknesses, a $1.37 million cash reconciliation gap and more than $3.3 million in capital asset adjustments.

Budget gap: The fiscal 2026 budget projected about $65.5 million in revenue against about $84.9 million in spending.

No sunset or targets: The measure has no sunset date, and the county has published no estimate of jobs per dollar.

Who pays: Gross receipts taxes fall hardest on lower-income households, the same working families already squeezed by rising costs and this year’s PNM bills.

This is not inconsistent with our yes on the state bonds. Those bonds were sized to replace retiring debt and keep the rate flat. The LEDA tax is new money taken from every purchase in the county, with no plan, no sunset and no clean audit behind it. Accountability first. Until the county shows voters the strategy, the books and who gets paid, the responsible vote is no.

One ballot, one standard

From the candidates to the last item on the ballot, we have tried to apply one test: does it make government more open, more accountable, and more useful to the people who pay for it? By that test, we recommend YES on Amendments 1 and 3, NO on Amendments 2 and 4, YES on all three bond questions, and NO on the county LEDA tax.

Each of these questions is decided by the votes cast on it, so do not skip the bottom of your ballot. Every vote counts.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. According to the Otero County voter guide, polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., any Otero County voter may use any voting convenience center in the county, and same-day registration is available. Confirm details at NMVote.org or with the County Clerk at (575) 437-4942.

item.title: Tigers Draw Chaparral Rematch to Open 5A Playoffs
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo Tigers will open the Class 5A state playoffs against a familiar face. The NMAA's bracket, released Sunday, seeds Alamogordo No. 5 and pairs the Tigers with No. 12 Chaparral in the first round — the same Lobos team they routed 55-7 just two nights earlier.

The NMAA held the 2A–6A brackets until Sunday after severe flooding in northwestern New Mexico forced schools to reschedule games. First-round games are set for Nov. 6–7. As the higher seed, Alamogordo is in line to host, though the game site and kickoff time had not been announced Sunday evening.

Friday's regular-season finale in Chaparral was never close. The Tigers posted their highest point total of the season, while the Lobos managed only a single touchdown.

Alamogordo (6-4) enters the postseason on a four-game winning streak, a sharp turn from a 2-4 start. Head coach AJ Cisco's team opened with wins over Santa Fe (41-33) and at Goddard (28-27), then dropped four straight to Clovis, Organ Mountain, Roswell and Artesia.

The defense drove the turnaround. After giving up 81 points in Week 0, the Tigers allowed just 47 total over their last four games — under 12 points a night. The offense has kept pace, putting up 48 against Deming on Oct. 22 before the 55-point outburst at Chaparral.

The Tigers are also in their first season in Class 5A. Alamogordo dropped down from 6A in the NMAA's 2026 realignment and joined District 2-5A alongside state powers Artesia and Roswell.

Chaparral (4-6) limps in, having lost six of its last seven. The Lobos started 3-0 before district play caught up with them.

A win would send Alamogordo to the quarterfinals against No. 4 Los Lunas, which earned a first-round bye. Beyond that, the top half of the bracket runs through No. 1 Roswell, which beat the Tigers 56-26 in September.

item.title: Haaland, Garcia Richard and Luján Rallied in Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, lieutenant governor nominee Stephanie Garcia Richard and U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján brought their closing pitch to Otero County on Sunday evening, Nov. 1, drawing a packed crowd to Rocket City Family Fun Center, the Alamogordo bowling and entertainment center run by the Mescalero Apache Tribe.

The stop was part of a swing through New Mexico's southern counties in the final days before the Nov. 3 general election. Garcia Richard told the crowd it was the largest turnout of any rural community the ticket had visited on the trip south. The rally began at 6 p.m. and, with the large and enthusiastic crowd, ran past 9 p.m.

The venue itself carried a message of partnership. In April 2025 the City of Alamogordo signed a management contract with the tribe's Inn of the Mountain Gods to reopen the 24-lane center, putting a tribal enterprise in charge of a prominent business off the Mescalero reservation.

Otero County Democratic Party Chair Joy Bordenave launched the program, and downwinder advocate Tanya Burns kicked off the evening. The Tularosa Basin sits downwind of the 1945 Trinity test, and local families spent two decades pressing Congress for compensation. New Mexico downwinders were finally added to the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act in 2025, when the expansion was folded into the federal budget bill. Senator Ben Ray Lujan has been a champion in that fight. 

Alfred LaPaz, a respected Mescalero Apache elder who served multiple terms on the Tribal Council and stepped in as the tribe's acting president during a 2013 leadership transition, opened the evening with a prayer offered in English and in the tribal languages. The Mescalero Apache Tribe is made up of three bands — Mescalero, Chiricahua and Lipan — whose roughly 5,400 members live on 463,000 acres in south-central New Mexico.

Mayor Sharon McDonald then gave the candidates a warm welcome to Alamogordo. McDonald, a lifelong resident and former District 5 city commissioner, was sworn in this January as the city's mayor and the first elected Black mayor in state history, and first Democrat to hold the leadership role in the city in over 3 decades. As a commissioner in 2023, she brought the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium's presentation before the City Commission, has led city wide cleanup initiatives and is recognized for her championing of transparency and true government accountability and inclusion, recently launching the Mayors Commission on Youth made up exclusively of youth. 

Sen. Ben Ray Luján delivered an energetic speech that praised McDonald for working toward unity and inclusion in "our house." He also heaped praise on Garcia Richard, New Mexico's commissioner of public lands, as the party's choice for lieutenant governor and at the end of the night emphasized the need to support down ballot candidates.

Garcia Richard matched Luján's energy, telling supporters the ticket was pleased by the size and enthusiasm of the Alamogordo crowd.

A former teacher, she served six years in the state House before winning the land commissioner's office in 2018. She launched her own lieutenant governor bid in 2025 but stepped away that fall to care for her husband during his cancer treatment. After his health improved, the Democratic State Central Committee chose her in July to fill the vacancy on the ballot left by Maggie Toulouse Oliver, with Haaland's endorsement. 

Garcia Richard has said she wants the office to act as a statewide ombudsman, with the governor's and lieutenant governor's staff keeping office hours in rural towns rather than only in Santa Fe. If elected, she would be the first Latina to hold the post.

Haaland Passion and Gratitude

Haaland spoke last, with deep passion and gratitude for the turnout. She worked the entire room, hugging and chatting with each person to make a personal connection.

A former congresswoman and U.S. secretary of the interior, Haaland won the June Democratic primary decisively and would become the first Native American woman elected governor of any state. Her campaign has centered on lowering the cost of living, strengthening schools and public safety, and has released policy plans on affordability, education, public safety and health care. She has also called water scarcity and climate paramount, and pledged to visit all 33 counties during the general election. She has visited Otero County at least 4 visits. 

Haaland and Garcia Richard face Republican former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull and his running mate, state Sen. David Gallegos of Eunice, to succeed term-limited Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham. Hull has argued that families are hurting under years of one-party control in Santa Fe. 

The final Albuquerque Journal poll, conducted Oct. 1–9, showed Haaland ahead 49% to 42% among likely voters, with a margin of error of 2.9 points (Political Wire). Haaland drew criticism in October for skipping a planned KOB-TV debate with Hull, citing a scheduling conflict (Albuquerque Journal).

Polls are open Tuesday, Nov. 3, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

item.title: Alamogordo Commission to weigh emergency declaration over Bonito Lake runoff
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission will consider declaring an emergency Tuesday over repeated flooding and sediment runoff that threaten Bonito Lake Reservoir, part of the city's municipal water supply.

Resolution 2026-36 is the only action item on the agenda for the 6:30 p.m. regular meeting in the Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St. Utilities Director David Nunnelley will present it, and staff recommend approval.

Repeated rain over wildfire burn scars in the Bonito Lake watershed has sent significant sediment and debris into the city's sedimentation ponds and the reservoir, according to an Oct. 30 staff report. The ponds were built to catch that material before it reaches the lake.

The city has a contractor excavating the ponds, but runoff is refilling them about as fast as crews can clear them, the report says. The resolution ties the storms to "the current strong El Niño period."

Recent storms have also overtopped a cofferdam, washed out roads and culverts, caused erosion and piled debris beneath bridges and drainage crossings, limiting access around the reservoir. Some repairs have themselves been washed out by later storms, and the resolution says the ongoing work is rapidly using up the money set aside for it.

The declaration would formally document the emergency and authorize staff to keep up protective work: clearing ponds, culverts and access roads, repairing washouts and protecting the reservoir. That work would remain subject to the city's procurement and financial rules.

It also asks the state, including the New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, to consider the city for state or federal disaster aid or reimbursement. Eligible work could include sediment removal, cofferdam and road repairs, engineering, watershed stabilization and source-water protection.

City staff would be directed to track response costs, contractor bills, equipment and personnel time. City Manager Robert Stockwell, or a designee, would be authorized to file damage assessments and aid requests.

The emergency would stay in effect as long as runoff and related conditions keep threatening the reservoir and city facilities. The agenda report lists no dollar figure for the fiscal impact. Passage requires a roll call vote.

With the city attorney post vacant, the resolution is signed as approved to form by Stockwell.

Commissioners will also hear from Angel Chapman-McDavid, CEO of The BASE Otero Community Youth Center, formerly the Boys & Girls Club of Otero County. The item is a presentation only, with no vote.

According to slides filed with the agenda, the organization traces its roots to a local Boys Club effort in 1967. Its board chose to go independent in 2025 and renamed it The BASE, short for Belief, Authenticity, Success and Elevation. A new CEO was appointed this year.

The center, at 201 Dale Scott Ave., offers before- and after-school care, full-day summer programs, field trips, leadership activities and family engagement for school-age children. The slides credit the DeLeon family with a significant role in establishing that permanent home.

The presentation lists 2026 milestones including newly acquired 501(c)(3) nonprofit status, two new vans for youth transportation, building repairs and a new website and mission mural. It reports a line-item annual budget exceeding $900,000.

Goals ahead include stronger reading and math support, investment in staff and curriculum, and more diverse funding.

Source: City of Alamogordo agenda packet for the Nov. 3, 2026, regular meeting.

item.title: Nagamine Makes Positive Closing Appeal in House District 51 Video
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — On the eve of Election Day, independent candidate Grace Nagamine has released a three-minute video closing statement in her race for New Mexico House District 51. She leans on faith, family and neighborliness rather than party as the first true DTS or Independent to run in a major position in Otero County. 

The video was filmed outdoors at night in front of a lighted white cross. In it, Nagamine thanks voters and asks Otero County residents to turn out on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

"This campaign has never been about red or blue," Nagamine says in the video. "It's always been about me and you."

Nagamine opens by marking the season. "Just the other day we were enjoying Halloween with our children and families," she says, "and then Sunday, I was sitting in church thanking God for all His blessings."

She describes months spent walking neighborhoods and knocking on doors. "I've had Republicans, Democrats and independents walking alongside me," she says, "and that right there is what this campaign has always been about."

She also speaks about her own hardships. "I know what it's like to struggle, to have nothing and to have to start all over again," Nagamine says. "I also know what it's like when someone reaches out a helping hand when you need it the most."

Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident and a certified nursing assistant. Her campaign website says she has survived homelessness and domestic violence. It also says she has belonged to Mountain View Church for more than 10 years. "I was born and raised right here in Alamogordo," she says in the video. "This is my home."

She returns to faith near the end. "I have always believed that God has a purpose for our lives," she says, "and I know He has carried me through every season of mine."

Nagamine says she did not enter the race "to fight over political parties." She says she ran because "our families deserve better."

"Our seniors deserve to be cared for, our children deserve to be protected and our communities deserve safe roads, reliable water and someone in Santa Fe who will listen and truly listen," she says.

Those themes match the priorities on her campaign website. They are roads, water, child welfare, senior care and support for military families, including those at Holloman Air Force Base. The site also says she will publish her capital outlay requests each session.

House District 51 covers Alamogordo and much of Otero County. Nagamine faces Republican incumbent Rep. John Block, who has held the seat since 2023. Block ran unopposed in the June Republican primary. No Democrat is on the ballot. Block’s closing salvo has been to latch on to Greg Cunningham. Also Block has focused on negative campaigning against his opponent rather than debating his voting record or the issues. He failed to join the community forum on the first Tuesday of November whereas most other candidates joined. 

Nagamine has opted to run a positive campaign and has been endorsed by multiple leaders across both parties as well as small business interests, environmental interests, farming interests, leaders of the faith community and state and federal officials. 

In the video, she asks voters to go to the polls Tuesday. "If you've already voted, thank you from the bottom of my heart," she says. "Take your family, take a friend and let's show up for our community."

She closes the way she began, by introducing herself. "I'm Grace Nagamine, your independent candidate for New Mexico House District 51," she says. "God bless."

The full video is available on YouTube.

item.title: Otero County Commission: Emery vs. Lambert
item.description:
Otero County voters will settle the District 2 County Commission seat on Tuesday, November 3, choosing between Republican Jonathan T. Emery and independent Evan Christopher Lambert Ross. Both men are running as outsiders against the political class. That shared message divided the New Mexico Conservative News editorial board, and this year it is not offering a single endorsement.

Some board members backed Emery for his decades in uniform and his willingness to take on his own party's establishment in the June primary.

Others backed Lambert, arguing that voters are ready to move past incumbents and party organizations altogether

Below is how the two candidates compare, drawn from their campaign websites and public statements.

Emery is an Air Force veteran who describes himself on his campaign site as an OEF/OIF combat veteran. He spent his career in local law enforcement, beginning with the Alamogordo Police Department in 2006 and joining the Otero County Sheriff's Office in 2009, where he rose from deputy to sergeant to lieutenant before retiring this year.

His biggest political credential is how he got on the November ballot. In January he challenged incumbent Commissioner Amy Barela, who at the time also chaired the Republican Party of New Mexico.

The race drew a lawsuit and a statewide debate over whether Barela could keep the party chair while facing a Republican challenger. On June 2, Emery won the primary with 879 votes, 51 percent, a 45-vote margin over the sitting commissioner and party chair.

Emery's website frames his campaign around "Faith, Family, Service" and conservative New Mexico values. His stated priorities:

Evan Lambert moved to Alamogordo from Bakersfield, California, in 2020 to care for his mother, a retired Navy chief. He is raising a young son here. He filed as a Declined-to-State independent on June 25, ensuring Emery would not walk into the seat unopposed. Last year he ran for Alamogordo City Commission District 2 and lost to incumbent Stephen Burnett.

He founded and leads Community Power New Mexico, a nonprofit that runs the Otero County Labor Hub, a free tool library and materials bank on Indiana Avenue. It also runs Building Futures, which steers at-risk youth toward the trades. On his campaign site, he says he will work with anyone regardless of party and does not want to be a career politician.

His platform centers on families, affordability, jobs and accountability:

Both men reject the label of career politician, both promise a more transparent county government, and both say District 2 has been governed from a distance. 

Both also tout grassroots, small-dollar campaigns. The difference is what each would do with the seat.

Two kinds of outsider

Emery's claim to outsider status was earned inside the Republican Party. He did not leave the GOP to fight its establishment; he stayed in and beat it, unseating a sitting commissioner who also chaired the state party

Lambert’s claim rests on standing outside the party system entirely. He filed as a Declined-to-State candidate and says he will work with anyone, regardless of label. One man is a reformer from within; the other wants to bypass the parties altogether.

Two kinds of résumé. Emery brings decades of institutional experience. He served in the Air Force, then spent his career in local law enforcement, rising to lieutenant at the Sheriff's Office. He also helped rebuild the county's network infrastructure and the dispatch center's technology, so he knows county operations from the inside.

Lambert’s experience comes from the nonprofit world. He built Community Power New Mexico from the ground up, running a free tool library and a youth trades program. Emery knows how county government works today. Lambert has spent his time working around its gaps.

Two views of public safety. For Emery, public safety means backing law enforcement and keeping neighborhoods safe, a priority shaped by years on patrol. He also says his work as a deputy showed him how mental health struggles affect local families, and he wants the county to support those resources

Lambert approaches public safety through oversight. He wants a transparency overhaul of the Sheriff's Office, changes to its hiring and public reporting, and an audit of the county's Flock license-plate cameras.

One sees law enforcement as a partner to strengthen; the other sees it as an institution to hold more tightly to account.

Two views of the county's job- This is the deepest divide

Emery's platform is rooted in conservative principles: protect taxpayer dollars, keep government efficient and focus on core services like roads, infrastructure and responsible growth.

Lambert envisions a far more active county. He wants a public land bank, a landlord registry that tracks rents, higher local wage standards with county offsets for local employers, and public investment steered toward keeping money in Otero County. 

For voters worried about spending, Emery's approach is the safer bet.

For voters worried about rent and wages, Lambert offers more concrete proposals.

Two views of representation. Both candidates say District 2 has been governed from a distance.

Emery's answer is better leadership: a commissioner who listens and answers to the people.

Lambert’s answer is structural. He would expand the commission from three seats to five, giving Chaparral and the Mescalero Apache Reservation their own voice, and create community councils that help set the county agenda before votes are taken.

Emery would change who sits in the chair

Lambert would change how many chairs there are and who sets the agenda.

The case for Emery. Board members who favored Emery pointed first to his law enforcement record. Otero County is a public-safety county, and few candidates know its roads, dispatch systems and deputies as well as a retiring sheriff's lieutenant.

They also credited his primary run. Emery took on the Republican establishment on principle, challenging a sitting commissioner who also chaired the state party, and he beat the machine-backed incumbent. 

To these members, that is proof he answers to voters, not party bosses.

The case for Lambert. Other members argued that in this political atmosphere, a party label is itself the problem.

They want independents who owe nothing to any party organization and who focus on families, affordability, jobs and accountability.

To them, Ross’s housing, wage and transparency agenda speaks directly to working families squeezed by rising costs. They see his independence as the cleanest break from the status quo.

What the split tells us. The board could not reach a majority, so it is not endorsing in this race.

That split is itself the story. 

A year ago, the fault line in Otero County politics ran between Republicans and Democrats.

In 2026 it runs between voters and institutions. Emery's 45-vote primary win showed that Republican voters were willing to fire their own party's chair.

Ross’s candidacy asks whether voters are ready to go further and fire the parties themselves.

That is the real choice on Tuesday's ballot

A vote for Emery says the system can be fixed by putting principled, experienced people inside it, and he has already proven he will cross his own party to do it.

A vote for Lambert says the system needs to be rebuilt, with more seats at the table and more power handed back to neighborhoods.

Both men are betting that District 2 is fed up.

The only question is whether voters want a better steward or a different design.

Whoever wins, the message from Otero County this year is already clear: no seat is safe, no party is owed loyalty, and every officeholder now answers to voters who have shown they will act.

District 2 voters should weigh which kind of change they want, and vote on Tuesday, November 3.

This editorial was approved  by the New Mexico Conservative News editorial advisory board, whose members include two Republicans, two Democrats, one Libertarian, and one member who declined to state a party.

item.title: COMMENTARY: Today Is the Day. Alamogordo, Go Vote.
item.description:
Alamogordo N M- Every election season we hear that “this one matters.

Today, for Alamogordo and Otero County, it really does. The people we send to Santa Fe and the decisions on our ballot will shape our roads, our water, our schools, and whether our town keeps waiting for a future that never arrives.

Voting is the one moment when every resident has the same voice: the retiree on a fixed income, the young family at Holloman, the small-business owner downtown. It costs nothing but a little time, and nobody can take it from you except you, by staying home.

If you haven’t voted early, please make time today.

Voting locations

And the early numbers say this community is paying attention. Statewide Independents and Democrats are voting at a higher rate than in 2022, and total votes cast so far already exceed 2022, the last off-year election. 

Will that trend continue? That’s up to you. Let’s make it happen today, on Election Day.

Start with the facts

Before you mark your ballot, we encourage you to read the nonpartisan Alamogordo Town News Voter Guide, which lays out both sides of each issue without telling you what to think. It’s built for voters who want to decide for themselves.

Read the nonpartisan voter guide here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/15T7BLUbtTV_4abE6xiCmFr8K-FZF6U5W/view?usp=drivesdk

Where we stand

Our news coverage stays neutral. 

Our editorial page does not! 

Here are the positions of Alamogordo Town News on key races and issues, and why:

 State Senate District 33 — Liam Griffin: He has already shown up for this region, with largely unpaid legal work for families hit by the Ruidoso floods and 16 years practicing law. Rex Wilson is a serious, decent candidate, but voters, not an appointment, should choose who holds this seat.

Otero County Commission — No endorsement: Our editorial board split. Some members back Republican Jonathan Emery for his law enforcement record; others back independent Evan Lambert for his independence and his focus on housing, wages and transparency. Read both cases and decide.

 Amendment 1 (governor’s vetoes) — YES: Bills should not die silently. Governors should explain their vetoes in writing.•

Amendment 2 (school election timing) — NO: It removes the constitutional wall that keeps school elections off the partisan ballot and could open the door to partisan school board races.

Amendment 3 (university regents) — YES: Governors would pick regents from a qualified nominating committee list, with Senate confirmation still required.

 Amendment 4 (legislator pay) — NO: A paycheck without defined duties or accountability, and one that favors incumbents over challengers.

Bond Questions 1, 2 and 3 — YES: Senior facilities including vehicles for Otero County senior centers, library materials, and campus improvements including NMSU-Alamogordo, all while keeping the bond tax rate flat.

County LEDA gross receipts tax — NO: New money should not come before a spending plan, and the county’s audit findings and budget gap call for caution.

You may agree with us or you may not. Either way, show up.

House District 51: Why we stand with Grace Nagamine

We have been unapologetic in our support for Grace Nagamine in House District 51, and we stand by it today.

In our view, Rep. John Block has treated this seat as a stepping stone, using the position to build his own résumé as a political opportunist rather than to deliver for the people of Alamogordo

Representation is more than press releases and partisan point-scoring. It means showing up for the community you serve with authenticity, practicing ethical leadership, and conducting yourself in an open collaborative and bipartisan manner when listening to constituents in a way young people in this district can look up to

In our judgment, Rep. Block has fallen short every step of the way, blocking opposing voices and fighting dirty not the issues. We feel he makes a mockery of religion with his life choices and how he conducts himself and does not represent the best of Alamogordo with positivity and compassion. 

Grace Nagamine offers something Alamogordo hasn’t had in a long time: a truly independent voice.
