item.title: Block vs. Nagamine: Rep John Blocks Closest Race Yet
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M - Republican Rep. John Block won a third term in Otero County's House District 51 on Tuesday, but independent Grace Nagamine held him to the narrowest margin of his career. With all 31 precincts reporting, Block led 5,037 votes to 4,045, or 55.5% to 44.5%, according to unofficial Secretary of State results.

That 992-vote, 11-point margin is less than half the gap Block posted in either of his previous general elections. And Nagamine did it without a party line on the ballot: she filed as a decline-to-state candidate in late June, after Block had run unopposed in the Republican primary.

Nagamine was not on the ballot in 2022 or 2024. Block's earlier general-election opponents were Democrats Sharonlee Cummins in 2022 and Ashlie Myers in 2024. The comparison below measures how Nagamine performed against the same incumbent, in the same district, relative to the challengers who came before her.

A lifelong Alamogordo resident, Nagamine founded the charity Royal Angels and is a former Mrs. New Mexico. She ran on the district's aging water system, child-welfare reform and housing for military families, arguing none of them belong to one party.

Nagamine congratulated Block on his victory and said she supports the will of the voters. She thanked her supporters and promised to keep fighting for children and working families. Her message ended with a hint at what comes next: "Stay tuned."

Block's winning margin fell from 26 points in 2022 and 22 points in 2024 to 11 points this year. Nagamine's 44.5% share beat the 2024 challenger by 5.6 points and the 2022 challenger by 7.5 points.

In 2022, Block defeated Democrat Sharonlee Cummins 5,856 votes to 3,434, or 63% to 37%, a margin of 26 points and 2,422 votes. In 2024, he beat Democrat Ashlie Myers 7,514 to 4,781, or 61.1% to 38.9%, a margin of 22.2 points and 2,733 votes. This year, he defeated independent Grace Nagamine 5,037 to 4,045, or 55.5% to 44.5%, a margin of 11 points and just 992 votes.

Turnout matters for reading the raw votes. 2024 was a presidential year with about 12,300 ballots cast in the race, so Myers' 4,781 votes exceed Nagamine's total even though her share was far lower. In the more comparable 2022 midterm, Nagamine topped Cummins by about 600 votes while Block's own total dropped by about 800.

2026 figures are unofficial; 2022 and 2024 figures are certified results via Ballotpedia.

Nagamine's path depended on combining Democrats with decline-to-state voters and some Republicans. Early-vote data through Oct. 16 showed the district's ballots split 43% Republican, 40% Democratic and 17% decline-to-state, a closer partisan mix than Block's past margins suggest.

Nagamine’s campaign hit a cord of hope with many working class families and families with children whereas Block held enough of his base to squeeze a victory in a race he had to fight for. Alamogordo Town News congratulates the candidates and looks forward to covering Block in the new legislature in 2027.

item.title: Otero County and New Mexico 2026 Election Results
item.description:
New Mexico Democrats swept every statewide and congressional race Tuesday, led by Deb Haaland's election as governor, while Otero County stayed Republican down the ballot. Republicans won both contested county commission seats, and Rep. John Block held House District 51 in the closest race of his career.

Otero voters also rejected a proposed county gross receipts tax for economic development by nearly 2 to 1. Statewide turnout was 49.7%, with 726,684 ballots cast. All results are unofficial until the state certifies the canvass.

Democrats won every statewide and congressional race on the ballot. Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, becomes the first Native American woman elected governor of any state.

Haaland and running mate Stephanie Garcia Richard defeated Republicans Gregg Hull and David Gallegos with 57.2% of the vote. Sen. Ben Ray Luján won a second term with 63.2% over Republican write-in candidate Larry Marker. In the 2nd Congressional District, which includes Otero County, Rep. Gabe Vasquez beat Republican Greg Cunningham with 58.7%.

Down the ballot, Attorney General Raúl Torrez defeated Republican Samuel Kane, and Doña Ana County Clerk Amanda López Askin beat Republican Ramona Goolsby for secretary of state. State Auditor Joseph Maestas defeated Republican Joshua Lawrence, State Treasurer Laura Montoya beat Republican James Ellison, and Democrat Juan de Jesús Sanchez III defeated Republican Michael Perry for land commissioner.

Shares are from NBC News with about 98% of the vote counted. Elsewhere, Reps. Melanie Stansbury (District 1) and Teresa Leger Fernández (District 3) also won reelection.

Otero County went the other way at the top of the ticket: early returns showed Hull carrying the county by double digits. Final county-level totals for the statewide races were not yet posted.

Block won a third term in House District 51, 5,037 votes to 4,045 (55.5% to 44.5%) over independent Grace Nagamine, with all 31 precincts reporting. His 11-point margin was less than half of his 26-point win in 2022 and 22-point win in 2024. Nagamine congratulated Block, said she supports the will of the voters and pledged to keep fighting for children and working families.

Republicans won every county office, and the closest contest was the District 1 commission seat, decided by 333 votes. All 66 precincts reported.

In Commission District 1, Republican Christopher Wayne Glidden defeated Democrat Alan David Gonzalez 2,593 votes to 2,260, or 53.4% to 46.6%. In Commission District 2, Republican Jonathan T. Emery beat independent Evan Christopher Lambert 2,947 to 1,628, or 64.4% to 35.6%.

Three county officials won without opposition: Sheriff-elect Geraldine Yazza Martinez (R) with 12,475 votes, Assessor-elect James M. Bowman (R) with 11,736 and Probate Judge-elect Jessica Lynn Suggs (R) with 11,519.

Martinez, a Mescalero Apache tribal member, becomes Otero County's first female sheriff and its first Native American sheriff. Emery reached the general election by ousting Commissioner Amy Barela, the state Republican Party chair, in the June primary. Magistrate judges John Robinson Secrest III (Division 1) and Joseph W. Cutts (Division 2) ran unopposed.

Economic development tax fails: Voters rejected a countywide 0.125% gross receipts tax that would have funded Local Economic Development Act projects, 9,971 votes (63.2%) to 5,818 (36.8%).

All four constitutional amendments and all three statewide bond questions passed. Amendment 4 ends New Mexico's status as the only state that doesn't pay legislators, setting their salary at the state's median household income starting in 2029.

item.title: Unity over Division, Ethics and Positivity on Display at Emery, Nagamine Watch Party
item.description:
Election nights usually split a town into winners and losers, into the room that cheers and the room that goes quiet. Last night in Alamogordo, more than 140 of our neighbors chose to share one room instead, and it may be the most hopeful thing to come out of this election.

The party was co-hosted by two candidates who would never be mistaken for political twins. Jonathan Emery, a Republican with a law enforcement and military background, won his seat on the Otero County Commission after a tough primary fight against the state Republican Party chair. Grace Nagamine, an independent, took on Rep. John Block in House District 51 and came closer than any of his past general-election challengers. Their politics differ. Their campaigns did not. Emery ran on decency, ethics and simply being nice. Nagamine ran on redemption, family values and positivity.

The results were mixed. One candidate celebrated a victory; the other fell short. But you would not have known it from the mood in the room. The mayor took the microphone to celebrate democracy itself, reminding the crowd that what we share as a community runs deeper than any ideological divide. The mayor was joined by the former mayor and City Commissioner Stephen Burnet, a reminder that local leaders of every stripe showed up for the same reason.

Then each candidate spoke, and neither used the moment to talk about themselves. Emery and Nagamine celebrated one another and thanked the supporters who had carried their campaigns. In a season when so much political talk is built on tearing the other side down, it was striking to hear two candidates spend their big night lifting each other up.

That is worth holding onto. Campaigns end. Vote counts become official. But the people in that room will still be neighbors next week, shopping at the same stores, sending kids to the same schools and worrying about the same water system. Last night showed that Otero County can disagree at the ballot box without turning on each other afterward.

We don't need everyone to vote the same way. We need more nights like this one, where people of different views gather, cheer one another on and leave a little more united than they arrived. Congratulations to Jonathan Emery, to Grace Nagamine and to everyone who showed up to prove that democracy here is still something we celebrate together.

item.title: Martinez Officially Otero County Sheriff-Elect Highlights of Interview with Anthony Lucero
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Geraldine Yazza Martinez is officially Otero County's sheriff-elect after running unopposed in Tuesday's general election, and she says she is ready to take over the office on Jan. 1 — even if it means walking in just after midnight.

"The reality is setting in now, and I'm ready to move forward and do my best I can for the community," Martinez said in a radio interview with Alamogordo Town News on KALHRadio.org with Anthony Lucero after the results came in. "I'm truly thankful and blessed."

With no opponent on the November ballot, the outcome was never in doubt. But Martinez said the size of the turnout behind her left her "astonished by all the support."

Martinez said she had not yet heard from outgoing Sheriff David Black or anyone in his office about the transition. She plans to reach out to him directly once she wraps up her current duties.

If that doesn't work out, she said, she will go to the county manager and county attorney instead. "It's no big deal," she said. "If I go in there January first, right after midnight, then that's what I'll have to do."

Before she moves to the county, Martinez has work to finish at the Tularosa Police Department, which she has led as chief. The department's chief position is currently open, and she said she would like to see it filled before she leaves.

If it isn't, she said she will remain available to help the department with anything it needs. She also has open cases to close and "loose ends" to tidy up for whoever comes next. "My plate's going to be pretty full this next month," she said.

The real contest came in June. Martinez won the June 2 Republican primary for the open seat with about 54% of the vote — 2,818 votes — over Undersheriff Raul Robles (29%) and Cesar James Ramos (17%), according to unofficial primary results. No Democrat filed for the office.

A Mescalero Apache tribal member, Martinez is set to become Otero County's first female sheriff and its first Native American sheriff. Her career includes service in the U.S. Navy, stints as an Otero County deputy and narcotics sergeant, and posts as the first female undersheriff in Lincoln County and the first female police chief in Otero County.

During the campaign, she pledged to restore cooperation between the sheriff's office and other agencies and to rebuild public trust in the department.

Martinez grew up in Tularosa and has lived just north of the village for almost 20 years. She called her time leading its police department "probably one of the best things I've ever done in my law enforcement career," and thanked the village for the opportunity.

To the wider county, she promised to keep an open mind and keep learning. "I look forward to serving Otero County," she said. "I'm going to do my best to serve this community."

She closed by asking for prayers and thanking God for putting the job before her, saying she trusts He will "get me through whatever is presented to me in the future."

Martinez takes office as sheriff on Jan. 1, 2027.

item.title: Block Wins Third Term in House District 51; Nagamine Says 'This Isn't Over'
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Republican State Rep. John Block has won re-election to New Mexico House District 51, turning back a challenge from Alamogordo community advocate Grace Nagamine in Tuesday's general election winning in the tightest race he has ever won. 

Block, who has declined interview requests from KALH, instead released a written statement thanking voters and supporters.

"Tonight, the people spoke again — delivering a resounding victory and once again placing their trust in our movement," Block said in the statement, issued by his campaign.

Block wrote that his campaign stayed focused "through every attack, every distraction, and every attempt to divide us," listing families, freedoms, the economy, the military community, small businesses and the future of southern New Mexico as his priorities. He thanked God for "continued blessings, guidance, and strength" and pledged to "fight harder, work harder, [and] deliver even more for our district" in his next term at the Roundhouse.

"Tonight is not about me," Block said. He closed the statement: "Now, back to work."

Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident who ran as a decline-to-state candidate, spoke with KALH by phone after the results came in. She said she considered the campaign a win for the community despite the outcome.

"The rally of supporters and everybody that came together as a community — I was well received, and I take that as a win for me and for everybody else," Nagamine said.

Late in the race, Block's campaign sent a letter to voters raising past decisions from Nagamine's life. Nagamine said she responded by telling her own story rather than attacking her opponent.

"I didn't sling mud, and I'm very happy to say I ran a clean campaign, and that's what I said from the beginning," she said. "Your past doesn't define you, and it doesn't."

She said she "didn't take it sitting down" and credited her faith for carrying her through the campaign.

Nagamine said her coalition included Republicans, Democrats, independents and undecided voters who knocked on doors and made phone calls together. "It wasn't about politics; it was about people," she said of her team.

She also signaled she intends to stay involved. "I'm not going to stop this fight for our community," Nagamine said. "If Block doesn't represent the neighbors as he's supposed to, then I'll be right there to make sure that he does."

Asked whether she would run again, Nagamine said she would pray on it. "Time will tell, and God will tell me what to do," she said.

"This isn't over," she added in a message to supporters. "We're gonna do the work, and we're gonna come out on top."

Block, the founder and editor of the Piñon Post, was first elected in 2022 after narrowly defeating incumbent Rep. Rachel Black in the Republican primary. He won re-election in 2024 with 61.5 percent of the vote. House District 51 covers a large portion of Otero County, including Alamogordo.

item.title: Democrats Win New Mexico House Supermajority as Republicans Turn on Their Own Leadership
item.description:
ALBUQUERQUE — Democrats will hold a two-thirds supermajority in the New Mexico House of Representatives for the first time in decades after unseating four Republican incumbents in Tuesday's election. The results have set off a round of blame within the state GOP, much of it aimed at the party's leadership.

Democrats will control 47 of the chamber's 70 seats when the Legislature convenes Jan. 19 for a 60-day session, according to Source NM. The Albuquerque Journal reported it is the party's largest House majority since 1994.

Democrats went into the election holding a 43-25 House majority, with two seats vacant. A 47-23 split crosses the two-thirds line needed to override a governor's veto.

In every flipped district except HD-57, registered Democrats outnumber Republicans, Source NM reported. House Speaker Javier Martínez, D-Albuquerque, credited both the national anti-Trump wave and state Democrats' record in office.

Republicans had at least one bright spot. Heather Scott Ellison picked up HD-4 from Democrats, according to MultiState.

The House losses came on the same night Democrat Deb Haaland defeated former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull for governor. Within a day, Republicans were publicly blaming their own party.

Aubrey Blair Dunn, who ran for lieutenant governor this year, posted on Facebook that Haaland owed thanks to the Republican Party of New Mexico and a list of party figures. Among them were former chair Steve Pearce, Sen. Jim Townsend and former chair Amy Barela. Dunn argued the party fielded candidates too closely tied to President Trump in a state where he is unpopular. He also said independent voters broke for Democrats after the party attacked Republicans who criticized the president.

A graphic circulating among Republicans goes further, calling for every member of the party's executive committee to be fired. It lists campaign transfers that legislative candidates made to the state party and says most of those candidates lost. It also holds the party responsible for the campaign mailers and messaging. The dollar figures in the graphic could not be independently verified.

House Minority Leader Gail Armstrong of Magdalena acknowledged a disappointing night in a statement, the Santa Fe New Mexican reported. She said a supermajority means Democrats must take full ownership of the results.

Much of the criticism centers on Amy Barela, who chaired the state party until a judge removed her in May.

The ruling sided with three Republican candidates, including Dunn and gubernatorial hopeful Duke Rodriguez. They argued Barela broke party rules by staying on as chair while running in a contested primary for her Otero County Commission seat. The state Supreme Court denied the party's appeal on June 10. Barela also lost that commission primary to Jonathan Emery by 46 votes, the Albuquerque Journal reported.

First Vice Chair Mike Nelson took over after her ouster. Barela quickly launched a bid to win the post back, but the State Central Committee failed to reach a quorum to elect a new chair in June, amid a boycott by many northern New Mexico members. The fight split the party largely along regional lines.

In June, Barela told Source NM the party should focus on the election and turn to party matters in December. Party officers elected in 2024 serve terms covering 2025 and 2026, so a new leadership election is due. Some Republicans now blame Barela for the November results and oppose her return. Her defenders, including party Executive Director Leticia Muñoz-Kaminski, earlier called the effort to remove her a distraction from electing Republicans.

The practical power of the House supermajority is limited for now. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds in both chambers, and Democrats kept their 10-seat Senate majority without reaching that mark. Sen. Rex Wilson, R-Ancho, held his seat against Democrat William Neil Griffin.

With Haaland, a Democrat, taking the governor's office, veto fights between the Legislature and the executive are also less likely. The 60-day session begins Jan. 19.

For Republicans, the next test is internal: choosing who leads the party into 2028.

item.title: Local Media and the 2026 Otero County Election: How Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org Coverage Compared to Other Outlets
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — As unofficial results from the Nov. 3 general election settled across Otero County, attention turned not only to who won and lost but also to the role local media played in informing voters. Alamogordo Town News and its partner KALHRadio.org produced extensive coverage that included a detailed nonpartisan voter guide, editorial recommendations, multiple candidate interviews, and community forums. That output differed in volume and format from the election-night results reporting and candidate sketches published by the Alamogordo Daily News and other local outlets.

In House District 51, Republican incumbent John Block defeated independent challenger Grace Nagamine 5,037 votes to 4,045, or 55% to 44%, according to unofficial New Mexico Secretary of State results with all 31 precincts reporting. The 10-point margin was Block’s narrowest in a general election. He won by 26 points in 2022 and 22 points in 2024. Alamogordo Town News endorsed Nagamine in a late-October editorial approved by its editorial advisory board and published extensive policy coverage of her campaign, including briefs on CYFD reform, oil and gas revenue, and survivor protections. The same outlet also documented Block’s decision not to participate in certain interview or forum requests.

On the local ballot, the Otero County LEDA economic development tax failed with roughly 63% of voters casting “no” ballots. Alamogordo Town News had recommended a no vote after examining the measure’s details and local fiscal arguments. Statewide constitutional amendments and bond questions produced mixed results that largely tracked broader New Mexico patterns rather than any single local outlet’s recommendations.

Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org also hosted the Oct. 6 Voices of Alamogordo non-partisan candidate forum at Otero Arts as part of their monthly series. Candidates in contested races, including county commission and state legislative contests, took part in a moderated discussion covering data centers, infrastructure, budgeting and taxes, CYFD, and related issues. Audience questions were taken under rules emphasizing civility. The event followed a September forum on Bonito Lake access that drew a packed in-person crowd and more than 800 online viewers; city officials used that session to address public concerns and adjust earlier closure proposals. The full Oct. 6 forum remains available on the KALH YouTube channel.

Anthony Lucero of KALHRadio.org conducted multiple candidate interviews that complemented the written coverage. These included discussions with the sheriff’s race candidate, state legislative candidates, and others. Many of the interviews are archived on the Krazy KALH Radio YouTube channel. Combined with the 32-page nonpartisan voter guide published by Alamogordo Town News, the forums and interviews supplied side-by-side candidate exchanges and primary-source material weeks before Election Day.

By comparison, the Alamogordo Daily News maintained a live results page on election night and published short candidate sketches drawn largely from campaign materials, along with basic voting information and guides for Otero County races.

That approach provided straightforward access to tallies and candidate backgrounds. Other local coverage largely followed similar results-oriented patterns once polls closed.

Neither the Daily News nor most other local outlets hosted recurring in-person candidate forums or maintained an ongoing series of long-form policy interviews in the weeks leading up to the election.

Why local media still matters in a small market is straightforward.

Reduced staffing at many legacy newspapers has narrowed the volume of original reporting on down-ballot races, ballot measures, and local governance. Independent outlets that invest in voter guides, moderated forums, and recorded interviews expand the information available to residents who cannot attend every campaign event.

In Otero County, the combination of Alamogordo Town News’ written analysis and KALHRadio.org’s on-air interviews and livestreamed forums created additional channels for voters to hear candidates directly.

Whether that additional information shifted any individual ballots remains unknowable; the measurable difference is simply the quantity and format of local civic information produced before Nov. 3.

Unofficial results remain subject to canvass. Full returns are available from the New Mexico Secretary of State. The Voices of Alamogordo forums and Lucero interviews can be viewed on the Krazy KALH Radio YouTube channel.

This article draws on unofficial New Mexico Secretary of State results, contemporaneous reporting by Alamogordo Town News, and publicly available forum and interview archives from KALHRadio.org.

item.title: Gary Person Commentary: RPNM's November 4 Official Call: Where Are the Rules Committee and the SCC?
item.description:
New Mexico Republicans have just suffered significant election losses. Why, and what is RPNM doing about it?

The November 3 election saw Republicans lose the governor's race, all three U.S. congressional races, and four Republican-held seats in the New Mexico House, giving Democrats a 47–23 majority. These results should raise serious questions about the Republican Party of New Mexico's direction. Where was the statewide strategy? What support was provided to candidates and county organizations?

What worked, what failed, and what is RPNM doing to correct course?

Instead of concentrating solely on electing new party officers, shouldn't leadership also provide a public accounting of these losses and explain its plan for rebuilding the Republican Party across New Mexico?

On November 4, 2026, the Republican Party of New Mexico issued its official call for the January 9, 2027 state officer election in Clovis.

A review of the September 6, 2025 Uniform State Rules raises serious questions about the call's procedures, membership freeze, nominations and compliance with New Mexico election law.

Here is the chronological breakdown.

November 4 — Was the call premature?

USR 2-1-4(A) establishes the November 15–January 15 organizational election window. The official call was issued November 4, eleven days before that window opens.

Although January 9 falls within the permitted period, leadership must explain whether the rule governs the meeting date, the date the formal call is issued, or both.

November 4 — Why freeze the SCC membership 66 days early?

The call immediately closes the SCC membership list and establishes a quorum of 366.

USR 1-3-1(B)(i) authorizes freezing membership after an official call. However, USRs 1-2-2(C) and 3-3-1(F) address loss of membership eligibility and filling vacancies.

How will those provisions be reconciled during the 66-day freeze? Who verified the membership total and quorum calculation?

November 24 — What happens when election results are certified?

USR 2-1-3(A)(2) bases county SCC apportionment on certified Republican gubernatorial election results.

The 2026 results are scheduled for certification November 24. Will those figures affect representation, and when will any new apportionment take effect?

December 7 — Who authorized the nomination deadline?

The call requires state officer self-nominations by December 7.

Yet USR 2-1-4(A)(1)–(2) requires congressional-district caucuses to nominate their respective vice chairs, followed by statewide confirmation.

Does the early deadline interfere with those required procedures? The party should identify its authority for the restriction.

January 1 — Who qualifies to vote?

USR 2-1-3(A)(8) grants SCC membership to certain incumbent Republican officeholders.

With changes in public officeholders occurring January 1, will the frozen November 4 roster reflect the qualified membership on January 9?

January 9 — What about the counties?

USR 3-2-1(C) requires counties to hold biennial organizational conventions in odd-numbered years, electing county officers and SCC representatives.

The rules do not expressly require all county conventions to precede the statewide election. Nevertheless, leadership must explain what happens if a county elects new representatives before January 9 while the old roster remains frozen.

The call also promises special election rules without providing them. USR 2-1-5(E) prohibits special procedures that conflict with the Uniform State Rules.

New Mexico law, NMSA 1978, Section 1-7-3, requires political parties to establish procedures governing officer elections, meeting locations and notices.

The Attorney General's Opinion 24-09 confirms that political party rules cannot override applicable law.

Has leadership documented compliance with the statutory election-week and notice requirements, including any applicable publication requirements?

USR 2-1-8 establishes the Advisory State Rules Committee and its responsibilities concerning conformity of party rules with law.

Has the committee reviewed this call? Has it been asked to examine the disputed provisions? If so, where is its written explanation?

USR 2-1-1 makes the State Central Committee the governing body of the RPNM.

USR 2-1-5(B) even permits 25 SCC members acting together to call a properly noticed meeting.

Why have members not received a comprehensive, written explanation of these issues? Why were the 33 county chairs not given an opportunity to participate in the location decision?

The public record does not establish that every SCC member has remained silent. But it also does not provide answers to these legitimate procedural questions.

The issue is not who wins the January 9 election. It is whether the election follows the rules and the law.

Before proceeding, state leadership should publish the certified SCC roster, quorum calculations, legal authority for the nomination deadline, proposed special rules and a written explanation addressing the membership freeze.

And following the November 3 election results, leadership should also explain what RPNM is doing to evaluate its campaign operations, support county organizations, and address the electoral losses.

The Rules Committee should clarify the rules. The SCC should exercise its oversight. And state leadership should answer the questions.

An official call is not proof of compliance. Accountability requires showing that the rules have been followed.

Sources: RPNM Uniform State Rules (September 6, 2025), USRs 1-2-2, 1-3-1, 2-1-1, 2-1-3, 2-1-4, 2-1-5, 2-1-8, 3-2-1 and 3-3-1; RPNM Official Call (November 4, 2026); NMSA 1978 §§ 1-7-2 and 1-7-3; New Mexico Attorney General Opinion 24-09; New Mexico Secretary of State 2026 General Election unofficial results and certification schedule; Source New Mexico, November 4, 2026, reporting on state House election results.

item.title: Otero Arts Opens 2026 Members’ Exhibit Friday with Reception at Historic Artspace
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Otero Arts Inc. opens its annual Members’ Exhibit tonight with a public reception from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Otero Artspace, 1118 Indiana Avenue at 12th Street. The group show, a longstanding membership benefit, features more than 40 works by 29 local and regional artists working in painting, sculpture, weaving, ceramics and other media.

The exhibition fills the walls of the restored historic Woman’s Club building—a 1930s Works Progress Administration Pueblo Revival structure that serves as Otero Arts’ home—and remains on view through November 29. Works highlighted on the exhibition poster include pieces by artists Prather, Nichols, Allen, Pilgreen, Higgins, Roark-Diehl, Keller and Apprill, offering a snapshot of the range of styles and subjects represented across the full membership show.

The event is supported in part by grant funds from the Devasthali Family Foundation Fund, awarded with assistance from the Community Foundation of Southern New Mexico. Otero Arts, a volunteer-driven 501(c)(3), continues its mission of strengthening the arts community in Otero County and south-central New Mexico through exhibitions, classes, performances and free public programs.

The Members’ Exhibit is one of the organization’s signature annual events, giving member artists a dedicated showcase each November. For more information, visit oteroarts.org, email oteroartsinc@gmail.com or call 575-446-3880.

item.title: Tularosa trustees approve cell tower permit with conditions, adopt new dog ordinance
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees on Thursday narrowly approved a special use permit for a cell phone tower on Sunset Road, despite opposition from nearby residents. The mayor broke a 2-2 tie to pass the measure 3-2.

The trustees attached 12 conditions that Flagship One LLC must meet before it can receive a building permit. Several trustees said they voted with the expectation that the village would lose if it denied the permit and the company sued.

The special meeting also saw the board adopt a rewritten dog ordinance and approve an updated personnel policy. A planned closed executive session was dropped because the village attorney could not attend.

The permit, Special Use Application 2026-002, covers a tower at 44 Sunset Road. The site lies outside village limits, within the village's extraterritorial zoning area.

Before the vote, the mayor reminded trustees of what was at stake. "Remember, this is just a permit," the mayor said. "If they violate this permit, pull it."

One trustee acknowledged that residents near the site opposed the tower. "I understand that our constituents in that area are not for this. I understand that completely, wholeheartedly, and I appreciate the time and you guys coming and voicing that," the trustee said.

But the trustee said conversations with the village attorney pointed toward approval. "If you don't approve it, they can take us to court, and we're going to spend unnecessary money to be told we have to approve it," the trustee said.

Officials said radio frequency emissions could not be grounds for denial because federal rules deem them safe. Public dislike alone also would not hold up, they said.

Residents had submitted a petition with 198 signatures. One official said a petition would need signatures from close to three-quarters of the village to carry that kind of weight.

Another trustee noted that Otero County has no ordinance governing cell towers and the site is unzoned. "If we don't have a law in place already, it's kind of hard to say no," the trustee said. "We're going to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars in court on this. And bottom line is they're going to win."

Trustees stressed that the approval is binding only if the company meets every condition. "If they don't meet everything in this thing, then they don't get such permit," one said.

The Mayor Pro Tem read the Planning and Zoning Commission's findings of fact and recommended conditions into the record. The tower would stand 190 feet 10 inches tall and hold up to four wireless carriers. Key conditions include:

The company also agreed in writing to lease space to other carriers on commercially reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms. Fencing details must be approved by the village before construction.

Trustees adopted Ordinance No. 285, which amends Chapter 95 of the village code on animals. The rewrite covers general provisions, prohibited activities, enforcement, and dangerous and potentially dangerous dogs.

The ordinance takes effect five days after notice of its approval is published in the newspaper.

Before the vote, Trustee Chris Rupp asked the village's animal control officer, identified at the meeting as Dean, to explain enforcement on issues residents had raised.

Barking. The public nuisance rule is unchanged from the existing ordinance. Enforcement starts with a complaint and applies from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Barking generally must be excessive, lasting longer than an hour. A dog that was provoked will not be cited.

Licensing. Officers will not go door to door or into yards to check licenses. "Everybody has their right to privacy and their own residence," Dean said.

Instead, officers act when a dog is found loose. Owners get a warning and a few weeks to obtain a license at the police department, where proof of rabies vaccination is required. A citation can follow if they don't comply.

Aggressive dogs. Officials said the dangerous-dog provisions target dogs that run loose and chase people, not dogs guarding their own yards. Dean said a dog that is provoked, or protecting a litter of puppies, will not be deemed dangerous.

Trustees thanked Dean for drafting the update. "Having the firsthand knowledge of having to use this every day made this, I think, a little more easier for us to go through," one trustee said.

The board approved the ordinance on a roll-call vote. Trustees Bruce Wallace, Rupp and Otero voted yes; Trustee Garwood's vote was not audible on the recording.

The board also approved an updated village personnel policy, brought back after what the mayor called a mix-up over which version was under consideration. Mayor Deborah Cooksey Myers presented the request.

One trustee said the revision was "put in good legal terms," and credited Chris Rupp with the work. Officials said a personnel specialist working with the village attorney handled the editing. The motion passed without discussion of further changes.

The meeting then adjourned.

item.title: Alamogordo Commission Declares Emergency at Bonita Lake
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission on Tuesday unanimously declared an emergency at Bonita Lake Reservoir, one of the city's drinking water sources, after five storm events this year repeatedly refilled the sediment ponds that protect the lake.

The 7-0 vote on Resolution 2026-36 covers continued flooding, runoff, sedimentation, debris and erosion in the Bonita Lake watershed. City officials said the declaration lets the city apply for outside funding it could not get otherwise.

"This year we've had five different events," Utilities Director Dave Nunley told commissioners. Each storm, he said, "undoes everything that we continue to dig out."

The city has a contractor excavating the sedimentation ponds above the lake. The plan was to clear one pond and then move to the other, but the contractor "keeps having to go back," Nunley said.

So far no significant debris has reached the lake, and the city is still drawing drinking water from it. But Nunley said the city is "exhausting all of our funds that we have in place."

Lincoln County has already made its own declaration. "I think it's the fiscal and responsible thing for us to do as well," Nunley said.

The city is working with King Industries, which helped it recover from the Little Bear Fire and a later wildfire in the watershed. Nunley said the firm recommended the declaration, which opens the door to funding and to permanent restoration work through the Department of Homeland Security.

If funding comes through, the city would keep excavating after storms and would also build a more permanent sedimentation system. The goal, Nunley said, is a plan to clear the ponds on a schedule "instead of always being reactive."

Commissioner Al Hernandez made the motion, and Commissioner Warren Robinson seconded it.

The meeting opened with a presentation from Angel Chapman McDavid, CEO of The Base Otero Community Youth Center, formerly the Boys and Girls Club of Otero County.

McDavid said the board voted last November to leave Boys and Girls Clubs of America and become an independent nonprofit. Because the center is funded mainly by the state of New Mexico, she said, the change leaves it "only one entity to answer to" and lets it focus on local children.

The center has served the community since 1967 and will mark 60 years next year. It serves children ages 5 to 17, though most are 5 to 13 because the state child care subsidy ends at 13. It is open from 6:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. and offers before- and after-school care, summer programs and field trips.

McDavid, who started in May, listed recent changes:

The center runs on a budget of about $900,000 a year. It plans to renovate its back offices to add a multipurpose room and a staff break and training area, ideally by year's end. A new "Base Scholars" program will focus on reading and math.

Its main fundraiser, Winter Wonderland, is a Christmas tree auction with First American Bank at 5:30 p.m. Thursday, Dec. 3, at the bank. The center remains at 201 Dale Scott Ave. and has a new phone number, 575-488-BASE. Its website is baseotero.org.

Though no public comments were scheduled, Azalea Street resident Alexander H. Wilson, a retired Army veteran, asked the commission for a speed bump on his street.

Wilson said he first asked about five or six years ago, when neighborhood children were 7 or 8. The city put up a 20 mph sign instead. Now those children are 11 or 12, he said, and "they're jumping behind cars."

He said a child was recently almost hit, that a daycare also sits on the street, and that drivers are "flying up and down the street now."

"I'm putting an alarm out here right now," Wilson said. "Can't blow it off no more."

Wilson thanked the city for earlier requests it granted, including an alley light, a street light and the speed sign. He said he has picked up the paperwork to formally request the speed bump. City officials took his contact information.

In his report, the city manager Robert Stockwell said utility crews will now finish street repairs themselves after work on water and sewer lines.

Before, utility crews filled and packed the trench and then left the final asphalt to the street department, which already had a backlog of potholes. Now utility crews will lay the asphalt and concrete before they leave. Stockwell said residents should see torn-up streets repaved much sooner, and the street department can focus on failing roads.

He pointed to a recent project on North Scenic Drive. Crews installed 750 feet of 6-inch pipe to loop several dead-end water lines, which keeps water from sitting stagnant. They also repaired the asphalt and concrete, with little disruption to the area.

On the planned aquatic center, also called the natatorium, at least five general contractors are reviewing the bid. They have sent 79 questions, which the city will answer before bids are due. Bid opening is still set for Dec. 15.

Stockwell also plans to ask the commission on Nov. 17 to meet only once in December, on the second Tuesday. Special meetings could be called if urgent items come up. He said November and December are routinely slow months.

Commissioner Baxter Patillo said the city golf course "is looking the best it has in a long time." Staff said the agreement with the incoming golf course contractor has had legal review and will be signed soon. The handover will start either Dec. 1 or Jan. 1.

Patillo also asked about a lodgers' tax. The city manager said staff are still working out the finances and when the tax could be charged and collected. He expects to bring a complete proposal at the December meeting.

Asked about the We Grow Alamo survey, staff said it has about 250 responses and will stay open into early next year. The city's planning consultant, Bohannan Huston, presented housing survey results at a recent check-in and will meet with the city again later this month.

Another commissioner noted that November is Epilepsy Awareness Month.

A third commissioner said the public housing on First Street, which recently lost water for about two days after a major leak, no longer belongs to the city. It is privately owned, so the owners hired their own contractor.

The meeting adjourned after a motion by Mayor Pro Tem Josh Riordan, seconded by Commissioner Mark Tapley

All votes during the meeting were 7-0.

item.title: RPNM Rules Clash Emerges as Leadership Prepares for January Officer Election
item.description:
New Mexico Republicans are confronting a fresh transparency dispute inside the Republican Party of New Mexico just days after statewide election losses. The conflict centers on a clear mismatch between the party’s published Uniform State Rules and the eligibility language on the official 2027 self-nomination form for state officers.

On November 4, RPNM issued its official call for the biennial organizational meeting of the State Central Committee, scheduled for January 9, 2027, in Clovis. That meeting will elect the state chair, first and second vice chairs, congressional district vice chairs, secretary, and treasurer. The call set a self-nomination deadline of December 7, 2026, at 5 p.m.

The published Uniform State Rules, amended September 6, 2025, contain a straightforward 90-day requirement. Section 1-2-1(C) states that to vote in a party convention or central committee meeting, to be an officer at any level of the party structure, to be a delegate, or to be a member of a central committee, a person “shall have been a registered Republican, as shown on the official list of registered voters of the county clerk, for at least ninety (90) days prior to said meetings or conventions.” The same section emphasizes that the rules are intended to encourage “the broadest possible participation of all Republican voters.” No other continuous-registration period for state officers appears in the 42-page document.

The 2027 Self-Nomination Form distributed with the official call imposes a stricter standard. It requires the applicant to affirm that they “will have been continuously registered as a Republican in New Mexico for a minimum of twelve months and prior to November 4, 2026.” The form is signed by RPNM Secretary Kathleen Apodaca and directs submissions to Kathleen@gopnm.org or by mail to the party’s Albuquerque headquarters. It also requires a letter of interest, resume, or personal bio to be shared with the State Central Committee.

Corrine Rios, a former RPSC State Central Committee member, 2024 Republican primary candidate for New Mexico House District 57, and 2026 Rio Rancho mayoral candidate, has publicly highlighted the discrepancy

In recent posts via social media she asked who authorized the 12-month requirement, when it was adopted, and where the authorizing rule appears.

She noted she has raised transparency concerns with RPNM processes since 2022 and pointed out that registered Republicans are not required to be State Central Committee members to run for state leadership positions. Rios, author of Running Against the Machine, has argued that information about the January 9 election and the self-nomination process is not prominently displayed on the party website.

The eligibility mismatch adds to procedural questions already raised about the November 4 call. Gary Person’s commentary on the same date noted that Uniform State Rule 2-1-4(A) places the organizational election window between November 15 and January 15. The call went out on November 4, eleven days before that window opens. Person also questioned the immediate freeze of the State Central Committee membership list, the interaction of the December 7 self-nomination deadline with the required congressional-district caucuses for vice chairs, and the absence of documented Rules Committee or full State Central Committee review of the call procedures.

These process disputes arrive against a backdrop of long-running internal friction.

Earlier in 2026, RPNM Chair Amy Barela faced lawsuits from fellow Republicans, including gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez and lieutenant governor candidate Aubrey Blair Dunn, over whether her dual role as state chair and Otero County Commission candidate violated Uniform State Rule 1-4-4. A district court judge ordered her to step down from the chairmanship amid the primary; subsequent meetings to resolve the chairmanship experienced quorum failures before the matter moved to further litigation and party processes. National Committeeman James Townsend and other officers issued statements defending Barela’s status at the time. Post-election commentary from Dunn and others has continued to criticize leadership performance and call for greater accountability.

RPNM has not yet issued a public explanation reconciling the 90-day rule in the published Uniform State Rules with the 12-month continuous-registration affirmation on the 2027 self-nomination form, or identifying the specific authority for the stricter requirement. The self-nomination deadline remains December 7, 2026. The January 9 meeting in Clovis will determine the party’s statewide officers for the next two-year term.

Republicans who wish to examine the documents can find the Uniform State Rules on the party website and the self-nomination form through the materials accompanying the November 4 official call.

As Rios wrote, “This is YOUR party. These are YOUR party rules. And the rules should be clear and applied consistently to everyone.”

item.title: System in Crises: PRC Orders Timberon Water District to Show Cause
item.description:
TIMBERON, N.M. — State utility regulators have ordered the Timberon Water and Sanitation District to explain why it should not be fined, put under court order, or turned over to a receiver.

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission opened Docket No. 26-0000191 on its own motion. The order was signed Nov. 5 and filed Nov. 6. It gives the district until Dec. 7 to respond.

The order marks the first time the PRC has formally put receivership on the table for Timberon. The idea was first floated by a commissioner nearly a year ago. Under a show-cause proceeding, the burden shifts to the district: it must demonstrate it has not broken state law, rather than regulators proving that it has.

The commission cited four possible violations of the Public Utility Act and commission rules:

The district must also show why it should not face monetary penalties, mandamus or an injunction, or appointment of a receiver under state law.

Separately, the commission directed its Public Interest Advocacy Staff to investigate two questions. The first is whether Timberon followed through on the financial, accounting and engineering plans it filed in its 2023 rate case. The second is how it spent the extra revenue from the higher rates approved in that case.

Any factual claims in the district's response, or in replies to it, must be backed by sworn affidavit. The commission said it has not yet decided whether a public hearing is needed.

The district's show-cause response is due Dec. 7, 2026, and PRC staff must file a preliminary report on its investigation by Dec. 18. Any customer or other interested person who wants to join the case as a party must file a motion to intervene by Jan. 4, 2027. Replies to the district's response from staff and interested parties are due Jan. 6, 2027.

The order was signed by Commissioners Gabriel Aguilera, Greg Nibert and Patrick J. O'Connell.

The disputed fee dates to 2012. In a June 2012 letter to property owners, the district said a 2006 court decision had capped its property tax levy and cut its income. It said residents who benefit from district services should bear their cost. Timberon resident Michael T. Gonzalez alleges in a formal complaint that the fee has been collected for more than 14 years without PRC approval. He puts documented collections at $247,965.36 as of April 2022. The district has denied many of those allegations and disputes the commission's jurisdiction over the complaint. It acknowledges that it is regulated by the PRC.

The current order also reaches back to a 2023 rate case. That spring, the district told regulators it urgently needed higher rates and had found no other funding for capital improvements. The PRC approved interim rates on conditions, including an engineering report, a financing plan and a plan to put its books in auditable order. The commission closed that case in September 2024, finding the conditions met. The new staff investigation will test whether those plans were carried out.

Pressure built through 2025 and 2026:

November 2025: At a hearing on a separate complaint filed by former board member Mark Harding (Case 25-00011-UT), Commissioner O'Connell raised receivership. He said the utility was not functioning. Then-board chair David Cruey replied that the district needs $45 million to $50 million to rebuild its system, not a state takeover (Source NM).

April 2025 and April 2026: The district's annual reports to the commission came due. Neither has been filed.

March 2026: Gonzalez filed his complaint (Docket 26-0000053).

June 24, 2026: The New Mexico Environment Department wrote to the PRC asking it to consider all remedies, including receivership. NMED said its sanitary surveys found 17 significant deficiencies in 2022 and 11 in 2025. It cited water losses of 70 to 90 percent of production. It noted an August 2025 enforcement order assessing $62,620 in civil penalties, which the district has appealed.

Aug. 21, 2026: PRC staff recommended converting the Gonzalez complaint into a show-cause proceeding, citing "manifest and weighty public interest concerns."

For residents of the Sacramento Mountains community, the order follows months of service failures. One ratepayer complaint, forwarded to the PRC by NMED, described pipes breaking and taps running dry several times a month. It also described residents being asked to help dig and haul rock for repairs while still being billed. NMED said the district reported another outage on June 22 affecting about a third of its distribution system.

Local outlet 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News has tracked the district's troubles since May. Its reporting has documented:

Rates. A base water charge of $74.59 a month for zero usage, plus a $16 trash fee (May 2026).

Outages and an unreported violation. Some households reported going three to five days without water. NMED found in a June 9 notice that the district had not notified customers of a March drinking-water violation (July 2026).

E. coli. Fecal coliform and E. coli were detected during line repairs on Aug. 14, prompting a boil-water advisory that ran through Aug. 21 (August 2026).

Leadership turnover. Within about six weeks, the board's vice chairman resigned, its chairman announced his resignation, and the district's records custodian left (July 2026).

PRC jurisdiction. At an Aug. 6 meeting, PRC legal staff called Timberon the only political subdivision among roughly 26 water utilities it regulates. Staff said the district had opted into commission oversight and had drawn seven outage and service complaints in 2026 (August 2026).

This  outlet AlamogordoTownNews.org has also reported community allegations about a 10-year, $1-a-month lease of the district golf course and an unpermitted trash site. Those issues are not among the charges in the PRC order. The commission's 2023 interim order did require the district to explain how costs shared with the golf course are allocated.

The service failures have unfolded alongside a deepening governance crisis. It has included litigation, unanswered public records requests, leadership departures and attacks on the  local journalists of 2nd Life Alamogordo Town News covering the district.

A district that has been here before. District records include a court-ordered receivership and court-set interim rates dating to around 2008, according to a 2nd Life Media review. The same review found at least eight Open Meetings Act complaints filed with the state Department of Justice since 2023. In November 2025, the DOJ found the board had repeatedly violated the Act. The violations included closing meetings under invalid attorney-client privilege claims and disciplining an employee outside a public meeting (July 19, 2026).

Mounting litigation. In August 2024, the district's own law firm demanded $126,645.62 in unpaid invoices. It threatened to withdraw from all pending cases, including active litigation, if not paid. The district is also a party in a civil case in Otero County District Court, Massey v. Hanson and TWSD (No. D-1215-CV-202500808). Board agendas in August listed employee litigation matters, according to 2nd Life Media (Aug. 21, 2026). 

Records requests. On July 9, hours after publishing a story on the golf course lease, 2nd Life Media editor Chris Edwards filed an Inspection of Public Records Act request. It sought 10 categories of records on the lease, boil-water advisories and infrastructure. Records custodian Leo McAtee declared the request excessively burdensome and called it a "scheme." In emails, he said the district had no obligation to release records piecemeal and suggested the request should have been split into smaller ones (July 13, 2026).

Three days later, McAtee sent a partial response and committed to deliver remaining records by July 23. That deadline passed without production, and he left the district shortly after. General Manager Wendy Case later wrote that the office was still reconstructing which requests were outstanding. In August, the outlet reported the district's sampling plan still had not been produced. It said the district's responses blurred records that did not exist, could not be found, or were withheld (Aug. 2026).  2nd Life Media is considering litigation as most records still have not been produced.

Former board member Mark Harding has reported similar delays on his own requests. District defenders have said staff are overwhelmed by records requests (Aug. 20, 2026).

Resignations. In about six weeks this summer, the district lost three leaders:

Vice Chairman Caleb Flora resigned in mid-June.

Records custodian Leo McAtee left in late July. Case said he left suddenly after the negative exchange with 2nd Life Media regarding an IPRA request. 

Chairman Otis Price announced his resignation, effective Aug. 1.

None has publicly explained his departure. 2nd Life Media has said it cannot show its coverage caused any of them (July 27, 2026). Board member JJ Duckett, who had posted daily water updates on community Facebook pages, also stopped those updates in July (July 2026).

Pressure on critics and press. On July 28, a district agenda item on the $62,620 NMED penalties named two residents, Aaron Foster and David Hunter, in connection with the violations. Hours later, a revised agenda removed both names. Harding said neither man had anything to do with the fines. He also said Hunter had sent Price a cease-and-desist letter.

Days earlier, an anonymous social media page had begun attacking Edwards' personal history and other district critics. 2nd Life Media described the sequence as an intimidation campaign. It has not established who runs the page or any link to district officials (July 28, 2026) and has considered litigation. 

The outlet notes that other news organizations covering the district have not faced similar attacks. Source New Mexico first reported the receivership discussion in December 2025.

Disclosure: 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News and its editor are parties to several of the records disputes described here.

The district now has about a month to make its case. District leaders have previously argued that the core problem is money. Most of Timberon's lines date to the 1970s, and a full replacement is estimated at $45 million to $50 million.

The district had not publicly responded to the order as of Nov. 7. 2nd Life Media has reported that it has requested comment from the district board on related issues.

Any Timberon customer may ask to join the case as a party by filing a motion to intervene in Docket No. 26-0000191 by Jan. 4, 2027. The commission's records for the docket are available through the PRC's online case lookup.

item.title: Alamogordo Tigers Dominate Chaparral 54-0 in 5A First Round, Advance to Face Los Lunas
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo Tigers made a statement in the opening round of the 2026 Nusenda Credit Union 5A Football Championships, rolling past the No. 12 Chaparral Lobos 54-0 on Friday night at Tiger Stadium. The win improves Alamogordo to 7-4 and sends the fifth-seeded Tigers into the quarterfinals against the No. 4 Los Lunas Tigers.

Alamogordo’s offense clicked from the start in a dominant performance that featured a balanced attack and multiple big plays. Scoring unfolded as follows, according to live updates from Otero County Sports:

• Qymani Patterson scored on a 45-yard TD run (Russell extra point good) for a 7-0 lead.

• Nathanael Cereceres added a 9-yard TD run (Russell XP no good), making it 13-0 at the end of the first quarter.

• Tristan Bowman ran it in from 9 yards (Bowman 2-point conversion run good) to push the lead to 21-0 early in the second.

• Cereceres connected with Rudy Wolfe on an 18-yard TD pass (Russell XP good) for 28-0.

• Cereceres then hit Bowman on a 76-yard TD strike (Russell XP good), giving the Tigers a 35-0 halftime lead.

• Leyton Niland scored from 2 yards in the third (Russell XP no good) to make it 41-0.

• Rudy Wolfe broke a 51-yard TD run (XP good) for 48-0.

• Niland closed the scoring with a 42-yard TD run for the final 54-0.

MaxPreps reported Alamogordo piled up 351 rushing yards and 150 passing yards. Cereceres was efficient through the air (5-of-7 for 141 yards and two TDs), Patterson led the ground game with 110 yards and a score on seven carries, and Bowman hauled in 111 receiving yards with a touchdown. The Tigers had scored 54 unanswered points after previously beating Chaparral 56-7 in the regular-season finale.

The shutout marked a strong home performance for a team that earned the No. 5 seed after a solid finish to the regular season. Alamogordo will now travel to Los Lunas for a quarterfinal matchup set for Saturday, November 14, at 1 p.m.

Rest of the 5A First Round and Quarterfinal Picture

The first round wrapped up over the weekend with several decisive results:

• No. 8 Santa Fe defeated No. 9 Cibola 23-7 in Santa Fe. It was the Demons’ first home playoff game in 41 years.

• No. 6 Gadsden blanked No. 11 Mayfield 50-0.

• No. 7 Goddard edged No. 10 Highland 35-22.

Top seeds Roswell, Piedra Vista, Artesia, and Los Lunas all received first-round byes. The quarterfinals are scheduled for November 13-14:

• No. 1 Roswell vs. No. 8 Santa Fe (Friday, Nov. 13 at 6 p.m.)

• No. 4 Los Lunas vs. No. 5 Alamogordo (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m. in Los Lunas)

• No. 3 Artesia vs. No. 6 Gadsden (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m.)

• No. 2 Piedra Vista vs. No. 7 Goddard (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m.)

Semifinals are set for November 20-21, with the 5A championship scheduled for November 28. Los Lunas enters the quarterfinals as a dangerous No. 4 seed with a strong regular-season resume and recent wins that included a 50-0 victory over Highland.

For Alamogordo, the focus now shifts to preparation for a road test against a Los Lunas team that also features a physical style of play. The Tigers showed explosive capability in the first round and will look to carry that momentum into the next round of the Nusenda Credit Union 5A Football Championships.

Chris Edwards is the publisher of Alamogordo Town News and a longtime local sports and community reporter and author of several books on Alamogordo sports history.

item.title: Disagreement Isn’t Disloyalty
item.description:
Guest Editorial

By Dr. Stephanie Hernandez

Now that the election is over, I find myself reflecting on the part of politics I dislike most: how quickly disagreement becomes permission to tear people down.

During a social media exchange, I said I hated politics. The former chair of the Republican Party of New Mexico responded that it was a good thing because I wasn’t good at it. I believe that was intended as an insult, but it wasn’t. If being good at politics means insulting people who think for themselves, I can live with that assessment.

That exchange reflects a larger problem: treating shared party affiliation as an obligation to fall in line. Shared principles should leave room to question behavior and should never require surrendering independent judgment.

My upbringing and faith taught me to treat people with respect and let my work speak for itself. Public service taught me that accountability sometimes requires difficult conversations. We can question decisions and challenge conduct without resorting to degrading behavior.

Anyone who knows my fiscal conservatism won’t be surprised that I’m a Republican. I support the Second Amendment, lower taxes, a strong military, personal responsibility, and accountable government. I can hold those convictions and still cringe at something my own party says or does.

I registered Republican in 1995, at eighteen, the first in my family to do so. I came from hardworking, blue-collar Democrats who valued earning their way and taking care of their families, and I remain proud of that heritage. But I believed in a strong military and fiscal responsibility at a time when the Clinton administration was shrinking the military and civilian defense workforce after the Cold War. I couldn’t get behind that direction. Choosing a different party did not mean rejecting the values my family taught me.

Years later, I met my husband while he was working on my cousin’s campaign as a Democrat. Our conversations helped him recognize that his conservative beliefs, military background, and Christian faith aligned more closely with the Republican Party. Political affiliation should develop through thought and conversation.

My friends and family hold views across the political spectrum. I don’t vote a straight ticket. A party label gets a candidate my attention, not my vote. I consider candidates’ qualifications and look for common ground, even with people I don’t fully agree with.

Although my husband was deeply involved in politics throughout our marriage, I largely stayed away from any involvement. When I was city manager, former Mayor Susan Payne helped me recognize that my lack of knowledge about Alamogordo’s political history was affecting my ability to do my job. Like it or not, a city manager must understand the political environment well enough to navigate it while serving the community.

Susan and I were not close before 2023. We were still getting to know each other when tragedy brought us together as mayor and city manager after one of our officers was killed in the line of duty.

Over five difficult days, we found our rhythm. We both spent time with the family and supported our officers while carrying out different primary responsibilities. As mayor and a mother, Susan provided a comforting public presence. As city manager, I coordinated resources, supported our staff, and kept city operations moving. Our roles overlapped, and we trusted each other to recognize where we were needed.

That experience became the foundation of our friendship, and other challenges that year strengthened it. She helped me understand the history behind political relationships I had underestimated, and I came to appreciate why simply doing good work did not make me immune to politics. Our friendship never meant we agreed on everything. It meant we had learned to trust each other through difficult work.

As our friendship grew, I believe some Republican leaders and supporters treated our association, and our willingness to question leadership, as disloyalty. Susan and others who spoke against what they believed was wrong faced criticism that, from my perspective, was often harsher than anything I experienced.

This election cycle, I became more involved and openly supported candidates. Beyond my own experience, I saw disputes here in Otero County raised similar questions about party loyalty and accountability. The state party chair also served as a county commissioner. When she drew a Republican primary challenger, a dispute arose over party rules requiring her to vacate the chairmanship. She remained in that position until a judge ordered her to vacate the chairmanship in May. Asking whether party rules apply equally to everyone is a legitimate question of accountability.

The statewide response showed how quickly that argument turned personal. A state senator defended the chair and portrayed Republican critics as more concerned with displaying their power than winning elections. Yet person he was defending, had publicly criticized others for less, casting them as a minority blocking progress. Defending one faction while questioning the motives of another does little to build unity. The same standards should apply to everyone, regardless of whose side they’re on.

There were calls for unity, but the public exchanges told a different story. In May, a Republican candidate questioned the senator’s honesty or understanding of the rules. In October, a candidate for Republican Party chair announced he was leaving the GOP to register as an independent, while making clear he was not abandoning his conservative values. His decision raises a question: how many people will keep their convictions but walk away from their parties?

It doesn’t have to be that way. Researchers who study groups describe dissent as one of the “normal and healthy aspects of group life.” A party willing to examine itself has room to improve. But will the parties reflect on their own conduct, or are they more comfortable letting people walk away than making room for disagreement?

After researching independent voters extensively for a client, I understand the appeal of political independence and the frustration with being expected to defend a party. Disappointment with politics should make us more deliberate with our votes. It should not persuade us to surrender them.

Congratulations to everyone elected to serve. The campaign is over, but the responsibility to earn the public’s trust continues. That includes listening to people who voted differently, respecting disagreement, and working with others for the good of the community.

As citizens, our responsibility continues, too. We should stay informed, participate, and hold those we support to the same standards as those we oppose.

Holding leaders accountable should never be mistaken for disloyalty and blind loyalty should never be expected.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez is a Republican and former Alamogordo city manager, serving 31 months combined tenure.

item.title: NMSP arrests driver on DWI-related charges following three-vehicle crash that left 11 injured
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — A 24-year-old man is facing DWI-related charges after New Mexico State Police say he ran a stop sign and caused a three-vehicle crash near Tularosa on Friday afternoon that sent 11 people to the hospital, including two who were flown to El Paso.

New Mexico State Police (NMSP) arrested Oren J. Shanta following the crash on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. He has been charged with great bodily harm by vehicle (DWI) and reckless driving.

NMSP officers were dispatched at approximately 4:04 p.m. to the intersection of U.S. 70 and Old Mescalero Road, where a black Chevrolet passenger car, a white van and a silver SUV had collided.

When officers arrived, emergency medical personnel were already treating multiple patients. Fire crews worked to free three people who were trapped inside the van.

According to witness statements, Shanta was driving the Chevrolet northbound on Old Mescalero Road at a high rate of speed when he failed to stop at the stop sign at U.S. 70. His car struck the white van, which was carrying 10 people, and the silver SUV, which was carrying three.

At least six passengers from the van, two passengers from the Chevrolet and Shanta himself were taken to a local hospital for treatment. Two additional passengers from the van were airlifted to a hospital in El Paso.

While speaking with Shanta at the scene, officers reported detecting the odor of alcohol coming from him and observing other signs that led them to believe he was impaired.

After further investigation, officers placed Shanta under arrest. He is charged with:

Great bodily harm by vehicle (DWI)

Reckless driving

No fatalities have been reported. The current conditions of those injured have not been released.

Charges are accusations only. Shanta is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

Information in this article was provided by the New Mexico State Police.

item.title: Proposed Pecan Council Changes Could Shrink New Mexico's Voice
item.description:
New Mexico grew about a third of the nation's pecans in 2024, but a federal proposal published Monday would remove the state's guaranteed seats for pecan shellers on the board that runs the industry's marketing order.

The Trump Administration’s U.S. Department of Agriculture's Department proposed rule (91 FR 70809, Docket AMS-SC-25-0881) would merge the American Pecan Council's three regional sheller districts into one national district. It would also require monthly reports on pecans traded between handlers and add penalties for late assessment payments.

Growers, shellers and buyers in Doña Ana, Chaves, Luna, Otero, Sierra and Lea counties have until Dec. 9, 2026, to comment.

The Council voted 14–0 on Aug. 14, 2025, to recommend the changes, according to the proposal. USDA says the number of shellers has dropped from 50 in 2016 to fewer than 30 as of August 2025, leaving sheller seats hard to fill.

One national sheller region. Today, the Eastern, Central and Western regions each get two sheller seats: one for a sheller handling more than 12.5 million pounds a year and one for a smaller sheller. The proposal opens all six seats to any qualified sheller, regardless of location or size. Staggered two- and four-year terms would follow.

Monthly transfer reports. Handlers who pass pecans to another handler would report each month instead of once a season. The report would add the weight and type of inshell pecans moved. USDA notes transfers usually run November through February.

Late-payment penalties. Assessments unpaid 30 days after the due date would draw a one-time 5% charge, plus 1% interest per month on the unpaid balance. On a $1,000 assessment, that is $50 up front, then about $10.50 a month.

The National Pecan Shellers Association supported the sheller change, USDA said.

New Mexico ranked second in the nation in 2024 with 84.8 million pounds, 32% of U.S. production, worth $167.1 million at $1.97 a pound, according to USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service.

Arizona ranked third at 16.5%. Together, the two Western states grew nearly half the U.S. crop.

Under the current rules, the Western region (Arizona, California and New Mexico) is guaranteed two of the Council's six sheller seats.

Under the proposal, it would be guaranteed none. Western shellers would compete in a single nationwide vote of all shellers.

The seats are already hard to fill. In February 2026, USDA's call for nominees listed open small-sheller seats in all three regions, including the West.

The change could cut both ways. Supporters say open seats mean fewer vacancies and more sheller voices at the table. But with no guaranteed Western seat, the region could end up with fewer shellers on the Council than its share of the crop would suggest.

Doña Ana County alone produced 55 million pounds in 2024, about 21% of the national crop, making it the country's largest pecan-producing county, according to NMSU extension economists. Every southern county with published figures is on the list below.

In Otero County, bearing acreage held at 1,700 acres from 2022 through 2024, while output fell from 2.93 million pounds in 2023 to 2.26 million in 2024. Local growers would see no direct change, but buyers and handlers there would face the new monthly transfer reports during harvest season.

NMSU economists estimate every $1 of pecan output generates about $1.80 to $2.00 in total economic activity in the region.

Grower seats and grower regions would not change. New Mexico keeps its three Western grower seats, two for growers with 176 acres or more and one for smaller growers. USDA says the rule adds no industry cost beyond the late fees and interest.

Assessments are paid by handlers based on the weight of inshell pecans they handle. The penalties would hit only handlers who pay late. Whether any of that cost reaches growers through prices paid at the scale is not addressed in the proposal.

The proposal follows a separate vote by growers on whether to keep the marketing order at all. USDA held that continuance referendum July 6 through Aug. 3, 2026; the order requires one every five years.

Comments are due Dec. 9, 2026. Cite Docket AMS-SC-25-0881 and the Nov. 9, 2026, Federal Register, page 70809.

Comments are posted publicly without change. Background on the state's industry is on NMSU's pecan page.

item.title: In Memory of Samuel Firmin Aragon

item.title: In Memory of Faye Ragan
item.description:
Faye Ragan, a beloved wife, mother, and best friend, passed away on October 31, 2026, at home with her family. She was 78 years old. Born in northern Minnesota, her family relocated to Wisconsin where she graduated from Oak Creek High School. Following graduation, she enlisted in the Army where she met and married the love of her life and started a family in Wisconsin, before eventually retiring and relocating to Alamogordo. After a life filled with love, kindness, and laughter, Faye has now “retired from living” and been received by her Savior.

A creative soul and talented crafter, Faye loved making handmade gifts for others and was always ready to help those around her. She had a wonderful sense of humor, a love of animals (especially her fur-baby, Dallas), and a quirky obsession with making patterns in the carpet with her vacuum cleaner. A devoted child of God, a proud Army veteran, a popcorn connoisseur, an unsuccessful (yet persistent) gardener, and a loyal Minnesota Vikings fan, Faye brought her own unmistakable charm to the things she loved.

Faye is preceded in death by her parents Eugene and Lucille Turner and siblings Hal, David, Karen (Blake), and Jimmy Turner.

Faye is survived by her loving husband of 59 years, Johnny Ragan, her daughter, Michelle Ragan, and a host of other loving relatives and friends.

Though she will be deeply missed, the memories Faye created will live on in the hearts of all who knew and loved her.

The family extends our heartfelt gratitude to Faye’s caretaker, Victoria, and everyone at Ambercare Hospice for the comfort, compassion, and dignity they showed Faye and her family.

A private service and interment at Fort Stanton State Veterans Cemetery will be held at a later date.
